n: The WS-X90 access control policy and its procedures exist as one signed baseline in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), which rejects an unsigned or superseded revision at check-in, and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) assembles every technician procedure package from the current approved revision so a field package cannot carry stale policy. The policy carries an annual review record, matching the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-1, and the profile change of 2026-09-08 triggered an out-of-cycle review. What is missing: the AC-family procedures were written against the previous 74-control scope and have not been reissued for the 546-control effective set, so seven procedures currently lack a current owner signature. REQ-436 stays partially satisfied until that reissue lands. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Account create, modify, enable, disable and remove actions on WS-X90 exist only as calls into the account service on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013); the on-disk account store is sealed and a direct write raises an integrity alarm rather than taking effect. Each completed action is published as a structured record to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) over the platform management bus within 60 seconds and with no operator step, which is what removed the manual re-entry the previous ground toolchain required. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management
n: Temporary and emergency maintenance accounts are created by the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) with a hard expiry no more than 72 hours out, the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-2(2), and are disabled rather than deleted at expiry so their history remains reviewable during an investigation. The expiry is also carried inside the session credential, so the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) refuses an expired account even when the management link to LRU-013 is down. What is missing: emergency accounts opened directly at LRU-014 during a communications-out recovery are still stamped by the technician rather than by the controller, so on that one path the 72-hour bound is procedural rather than enforced. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Two disable paths carry AC-2(3). On the platform side the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) disables an account within 72 hours of expiry, of loss of programme association or of a recorded policy violation, the CNSSI 1253 parameter value, and stamps the triggering condition onto the disable record so the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) can report per-trigger counts. On the ground support side the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) runs a daily inactivity sweep and disables any account idle for 90 days, the CNSSI value for AC-2(3)d, while the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) refuses offline logon with a cached credential older than the same 90 days so a laptop kept off the network cannot outlive the sweep. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The audit write is on the critical path of the account change. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) builds an audit record naming the actor, the target account, the action and the authorising role, writes it to the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015), and only then acknowledges the change to the operator; if the LRU-015 write fails the account action is rolled back rather than completed unaudited. LRU-013 then notifies the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which is the off-platform read path for account history. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

End-of-work-period logout on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is directed by the WS-X90 ground support operating instruction, which names the end of a technician's standard work period as the logout point, matching the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-2(5). LRU-017 makes the behaviour visible by showing the next technician how many sessions were left open at the previous shift change. What is missing: the requirement is carried procedurally. Neither station enforces a shift-boundary logout, and the open-session count is informational rather than blocking, so REQ-442 is verified by interview and by the shift-change count rather than by an enforced control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 carries privilege in named roles rather than on accounts. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) holds the four approved privileged roles and refuses to set a privilege attribute directly on an account, and the Mission Computer (LRU-001) accepts a privileged operation only when the presented role is one of those four. What is missing: membership change review is a manual checklist held by the System Security Engineer rather than a gate in the tooling, so a membership change can reach a mission load before its review entry is written. Closing that is tracked against the same work item as REQ-454. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Restrictions on Use of Shared and Group Accounts
n: WS-X90 runs one shared account and no group accounts: the flight line pre-launch check account terminated at the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014). Its two permitted conditions are that a named technician signs it out for a single sortie turn and that the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) tags every action taken under it with that technician's individual identifier, so the shared credential never breaks individual attribution. What is missing: the sign-out register is electronic at one of the three support sites and on paper at the other two, so the reviewer cannot reconcile sign-out to action without a site visit. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Usage conditions are designed and not yet enforced. The approved design binds each privileged mission account to a permitted mission phase, a permitted ground station identity and a permitted time window, held with the account record and evaluated by the Mission Computer (LRU-001) at authentication; the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) will apply the mission-phase condition a second time at the payload command boundary so a session that survives a phase change cannot keep commanding. Enforcement is scheduled for the 4.4 mission software build with an accepted entry criterion; nothing is fielded today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Atypical usage detection is a design on paper. The WS-X90 log analytics design record defines the per-account pattern as ground station, time of day and command class, with a threshold for each, to be evaluated by the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) against the account action and authentication streams it already receives, and to be raised to the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) as an analyst review item. The correlation rule set has a dated build item and a named owner; no rules are fielded and no alerts are produced today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A high-risk determination from the programme security office is entered against the individual on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), which then disables every account that individual holds within 30 minutes, the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-2(13), and drives the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) to revoke their provisioning credential in the same run. What is missing: the determination arrives by email and is keyed in by an operator, so the 30-minute clock is measured from entry rather than from issue. An authenticated intake feed from the security office is the open item behind REQ-447. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 is a non-discretionary system everywhere it matters. The approved design confines discretionary grants to draft mission plans held on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), where a plan author may grant read access on their own draft to another named author and nothing else; the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) refuses a discretionary grant on an approved release baseline, on signed configuration or on any airborne object, and no LRU on the aircraft implements a discretionary grant at all. The draft-plan grant mechanism is designed and scheduled; today plan sharing is done by copying, which the design replaces. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-4 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) is a default-deny inspection point: a flow it cannot inspect does not leave the boundary. Three encrypted tunnels are approved, and for those the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) terminates the tunnel and presents the plaintext to the gateway inspection path before release, so approved encryption does not become an inspection bypass; a flow whose key is not held by LRU-003 is blocked outright. What is missing: the terminate-on-failure path is implemented for TCP-bearing tunnels only. A UDP-bearing tunnel that fails inspection is dropped packet by packet but the session is not torn down inside the 5-second bound REQ-449 states. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Physical or Logical Separation of Information Flows
n: Planned: Mission, payload and maintenance flows are separated on the internal segment.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-6 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 enumerates its security functions rather than inferring them. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) holds the list — key use requests to the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), audit configuration, access policy load and boot policy change — and authorises each one only to the role named against it in the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) role table, which LRU-001 reads live so a role change takes effect without a software reload. LRU-003 does not trust that decision: it re-checks the presented role against its own copy of the authorisation map before performing a key operation, so a compromise of the mission partition does not by itself yield key use. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Privileged role holders on WS-X90 are issued two accounts, not one: the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) creates the privileged role account and its non-privileged counterpart in a single transaction, so a privileged role cannot exist without the everyday account that keeps it out of nonsecurity work. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) then refuses to open mission planning, telemetry review or documentation under a privileged role, which is the class of function the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-6(2) reserves. What is missing: eleven legacy engineering accounts predate the paired issue and still carry both uses. They are on a dated exception list with a closure date and are the residual behind REQ-451. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Only one network path may carry a privileged command across the WS-X90 boundary: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) forwards privileged traffic solely to the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and drops a privileged command arriving on any other interface without forwarding it, so there is one place to review rather than a policy per interface. Each privileged command that reaches LRU-014 over the network carries the operational need code recorded in the system security plan. What is missing: LRU-014 records the need code but does not yet validate it against the approved list, so an unrecognised code is logged rather than refused. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Privileged roles on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) are restricted to the approved privileged-personnel list, and the check happens at assignment rather than at review: LRU-013 refuses to bind a role to an identity that is not on the current list, so an off-list assignment cannot exist even briefly. LRU-014 accepts privileged role assertions only for identities LRU-013 has bound. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Privileged assignment review on WS-X90 is evidence-led rather than list-led. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) builds the review worksheet by joining each holder's assignment to the preceding 180 days of their privileged activity drawn from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), so the System Security Engineer judges continued need against what the holder actually did rather than against the role name. Reviews run at least every 180 days and on each role definition change. What is missing: reduction to non-privileged on non-reconfirmation is a manual action today; the tooling flags the unreconfirmed assignment but does not itself downgrade it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Execution privilege on WS-X90 is fixed at signing time, not at load time. The Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) records a maximum privilege level for each signed mission software image in its manifest, and the Mission Computer (LRU-001) starts the image at that level and denies any request the image makes to raise its own privilege above it, so a library invoked by a low-privilege user cannot execute above that user. What is missing: two of the three third-party mission libraries ship without a manifest privilege level and still run at the mission service level. Both are on a dated list and the supplier manifests are scheduled for the next delivery. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Privileged function use is logged at the point of execution on both LRUs that host privileged functions. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) each emit a record naming the function, the role, the account and the outcome, and the record is produced on the denial path with the same fields as on the success path, so a probing sequence of refused privileged calls is as visible as a successful one. Records reach the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which is where the enumerated privileged function list is reconciled against what was actually observed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Prohibit Non-privileged Users from Executing Privileged Functions
n: The Mission Computer (LRU-001) refuses a privileged function invoked from a non-privileged session on every path into it, including the mission scripting interface, which is checked at dispatch rather than at parse so a script cannot smuggle a privileged call through a data argument. The Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) enforces the same rule again at its own boundary: a payload configuration command with no privileged role assertion is rejected there, so the payload side does not inherit its safety from LRU-001 having filtered correctly. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-7 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-8 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Both WS-X90 session terminators cap concurrency at three. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) apply a maximum of 3 concurrent sessions to all accounts, the CNSSI 1253 parameter values for AC-10, with no privileged or service account exemption, and they refuse the fourth session with an explicit reason rather than displacing an existing one, so an attacker cannot use a new session to evict an operator mid-task. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-11 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

On session lock the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) hand the whole framebuffer to an opaque lock surface that renders no mission data, no account name and no window titles, and the compositor does not present the prior framebuffer between successful reauthentication and unlock, which closes the brief-flash exposure found on the previous ground software build. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-12 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Logout on WS-X90 is a session-wide teardown, not a screen change. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) expose the logout action on every authenticated screen, and the action terminates the session against all resources it reached, which is the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-12(1): downstream maintenance sessions the session opened on other LRUs are closed by session identifier, and Configuration Repository handles are released within 5 seconds. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) display an explicit termination message on every session end and distinguish the three causes — user logout, inactivity and administrative disconnect — so a technician who returns to a station can tell an idle timeout from an administrator cutting the session. The message is held on screen until the next authentication attempt rather than cleared on a timer. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Permitted Actions Without Identification or Authentication
n: WS-X90 permits two actions without identification or authentication, both on the payload side and both chosen because an authentication dependency would be a safety hazard: assertion of the payload-safe state at the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) through the physical safing lever, which must work with the platform unpowered, and read-only display of the payload built-in-test summary on the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) front panel. Both are recorded in the system security plan with their rationale. What is missing: the LRU-012 front panel also renders the last commanded payload state, which is outside the approved action set. Its removal is scheduled and is the residual behind REQ-462. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Attribute binding is designed across two boundaries and fielded at neither. At rest and in process, the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) will bind classification and releasability attributes to each mission data object at write, and the Mission Computer (LRU-001) will carry the pair with the object so the binding survives a copy between mission partitions, with attribute changes audited on the existing account-audit path. In transmission, the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) will carry the same attributes with every object crossing them, and LRU-007 will drop an outbound object whose attributes are missing or outside the approved marking set rather than releasing it unmarked. Permitted values are the approved WS-X90 marking set, which is reviewed for applicability every 90 days per the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-16f; the mechanism is scheduled for the 4.4 build. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No personnel-applied attribute association workflow exists on WS-X90. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) will carry it once the attribute mechanism behind REQ-463 and REQ-464 is fielded, since there is nothing for a person to associate or maintain until an attribute exists to hold. REQ-465 is carried unimplemented in the plan of action and no coverage is claimed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Consistent interpretation is a single-artefact problem on WS-X90 and is designed as one. A single signed attribute dictionary, carrying a version field, will be issued to the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010), the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009), so the encoding cannot drift per LRU as it did across the earlier payload builds; a version mismatch between two LRUs halts attribute-bearing traffic between them rather than letting one side guess. The dictionary format is approved and its distribution rides the existing signed configuration path; nothing is fielded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AC-17 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Remote maintenance is watched live rather than reconstructed afterwards. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) records the start, end, source identity and command set of every remote session and streams those records to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) while the session is open, which is what makes the AC-17(9) cut action useful — an analyst can see a session and end it. What is missing: live streaming covers the command channel; the file transfer channel is still written to the session record and shipped at close, so a transfer in progress is not visible at LRU-018 until it finishes. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Protection of Confidentiality and Integrity Using Encryption
n: Remote maintenance sessions terminate at the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) inside a protected session whose confidentiality and integrity protection is performed entirely by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003); key material never leaves LRU-003 and no session key is written to LRU-014 storage, so recovering the gateway yields no way to replay a captured session. LRU-014 refuses to establish a session when LRU-003 reports a degraded key state rather than falling back to a weaker protection profile. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has one way in. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) is the only externally reachable LRU and forwards remote access solely to the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014); no other LRU exposes an externally reachable listening service, which is asserted in the approved network baseline and verified by the boundary scan that runs against each release. A deviation is raised as a configuration finding against CM rather than being absorbed as a gateway rule change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Remote privileged access exists on two paths, both bounded. On the maintenance path the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) admits a privileged command from a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) only when the command is on the approved remote-privileged list, the laptop presents a current device attestation, and the session falls inside a scheduled maintenance window; the window test was promoted from advisory to a blocking admission decision on 2026-11-14, so a command failing any one of the three is now refused with a reason code rather than logged and executed. On the mission network path, remote privileged access to the Mission Computer (LRU-001) through the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) is limited to two documented operational needs, in-flight security policy reload and audit configuration recovery. One gap keeps this record short of complete: the need code is written into the LRU-007 session record by convention and is not a required field, so a session can still be recorded without one. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Information about how WS-X90 remote access works is held as controlled material, not as engineering reference. The gateway rule set, the device attestation scheme and the approved command lists live in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) behind an access list naming only the security engineering and platform roles, and the on-platform copy sits in a Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) partition that a maintenance session cannot read, so a technician with a live session cannot read the rules that constrain them. What is missing: two supplier design packages describing the attestation scheme are still on the general engineering share; they are listed with a migration date. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

One operator action cuts remote access. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) terminates every live remote session and stops accepting new ones, and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) stops forwarding remote access traffic within 30 seconds of the same action, with neither LRU requiring a reboot, so the cut is usable during a mission rather than only on the ground. What is missing: restoring access requires a manual configuration edit at LRU-007, so the action is not reversible from the operator control that issued it, and a restore therefore needs a second person. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Remote commands over the tactical data link are authenticated twice on WS-X90. The Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) hands each command's authentication tag to the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and passes the command on only if the tag verifies, and the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) verifies the same tag again before acting on a payload command, so a compromised radio cannot inject payload commands on its own authority. Failures are discarded and counted at both points, and the counters are readable in the maintenance download. What is missing: the second verification at LRU-010 covers payload commands but not payload configuration reads, which are still verified only at LRU-008. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is the only mobile device in the WS-X90 boundary and is treated as one. Its configuration and connection requirements are held as a signed baseline in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020); LRU-019 reports its configuration hash at each connection, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) admits it only when it is on the approved device register and the reported hash matches the signed baseline, refusing and logging otherwise. What is missing: the baseline covers in-hangar use fully but the annex governing use outside controlled maintenance areas is drafted and unapproved, and the per-activity release by a named authorising engineer is recorded in the maintenance plan rather than enforced at the gateway. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every enrolled Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) uses full-device encryption with the key bound to platform hardware rather than to a user passphrase alone, covering all mobile computers and devices that process organisation data, which is the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-19(5). Storage lifted from a powered-off laptop yields no readable programme data on another host, which is the acceptance condition the fleet is checked against at each provisioning cycle. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Information sharing on WS-X90 is a log-export question, not a mission-data one: the only outbound sharing path is a security log extract from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) to a partner programme. The approved design gives the releasing official one view showing the partner's access authorisations beside the marking of every record in the extract, so the comparison is made against the extract in hand rather than a policy memory, with the approved sharing circumstances held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). The circumstances are recorded; the comparison view is designed and not yet built, and it depends on the AC-16 marking work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 operates no publicly accessible system. The only public release path is the programme's unclassified support documentation set, staged in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and released through the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), and the approved approach names a single release official who reviews each item before staging and re-reviews the released set quarterly or as new information is posted, which is the CNSSI 1253 parameter value for AC-22. The release official is named and the staged set has been identified; the quarterly re-review has an owner and a scheduled first run but has not yet been performed on the expanded scope. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No data mining or bulk extraction detection is implemented on WS-X90. The Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) both enforce per-role access but neither applies a query rate ceiling, a per-role extraction volume limit, nor alerting on a sequential full-set read, so an authorised account can enumerate a whole store within its own authorisation without raising anything. The technique set is drafted, REQ-480 is carried in the plan of action, and no coverage is claimed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 relies on the Aurora enterprise awareness and training policy and has no system-level policy or procedure set of its own. The planned build issues a WS-X90 policy set to all personnel holding a WS-X90 account, the dissemination scope the CNSSI 1253 parameter for AT-1 sets, holds it signed in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), reviews it at least annually and after any AT-family assessment finding, and records the acknowledged revision per account holder so dissemination is a record rather than an assertion. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Aurora runs general security awareness training that WS-X90 personnel attend, but no WS-X90-specific literacy content exists and no account gate reads a completion date. The planned build makes completion a precondition for first enablement of a Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) or Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) account and at least annually thereafter, which is the CNSSI 1253 frequency for AT-2, adds a thirty-day retraining trigger on platform changes that alter mission data or removable media handling, and requires the course revision notes to name the incident or change that prompted each update. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No WS-X90 insider threat module has been written. The planned content is specific rather than generic: it names the indicators that arise in this system, requests to bypass the maintenance session record, attempts to widen a bounded maintenance task, and removal of platform data outside the approved transfer path, and it states that the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) retains the session record a report will be checked against. Recognition and the reporting path are both to be tested by sampling rather than by course completion alone. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Social engineering content is covered only by the Aurora enterprise course and no exercise has been run against WS-X90 personnel. The planned build trains Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) account holders to refuse out-of-band requests for provisioning material, session credentials or baseline identifiers regardless of the claimed requester, adds social mining content covering the collection of unclassified fragments about roles and schedules, and runs at least one recorded refusal exercise per year in which both the refusal and the report are scored. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Suspicious Communications and Anomalous System Behavior
n: WS-X90 has no published anomalous-behaviour indicator set, so operators are trained on generic guidance that does not map to what this platform actually shows them. The planned build publishes an indicator set drawn from the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) plausibility-reject classes, the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) out-of-envelope health values and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) alert classes, trains against it with a one-hour reporting expectation, and gates unsupervised mission shifts on completion. Publishing the indicator set is the prerequisite and has not started. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No advanced persistent threat literacy content exists for WS-X90 and the topic is not covered by the general Aurora literacy course. Long-dwell access and the abuse of legitimate maintenance and update paths for persistence are the two behaviours most relevant to this platform and neither is taught. No material has been drafted and no personnel have received training on it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Threat information reaches the WS-X90 engineering team but does not reach the people operating the system, and no bulletin is issued. The planned build produces a quarterly WS-X90 threat bulletin from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) alert history and the ground-segment feed, and requires each bulletin to be reflected in a dated revision of the operating instructions in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), so the current threat picture shows up in how the system is run and not only in a training record. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Role-based training is real for two of the four privileged roles. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) checks a current maintenance-role completion date before enabling a technician account, and Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) sessions inherit that decision, so an untrained technician cannot get in. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) operator curriculum is written and authorisations are recorded against it. Two gaps remain: LRU-014 does not disable an account when the training record lapses after enablement, so the twelve-month CNSSI 1253 frequency for AT-3 is enforced at the door and not continuously, and no curriculum has been written for the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) analyst role. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Integration bay personnel receive a facility induction that mentions fire and power equipment but is not recorded as environmental control training and is not repeated. The planned build gives everyone with unescorted access to the bay holding the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) units initial and at least annual training on the fire detection and suppression equipment, the emergency power cut-off and the environmental alarms, which is the CNSSI 1253 frequency for AT-3(1), and adds the shutdown order that protects platform state before power is removed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Physical security training for WS-X90 is currently the site induction only, which does not cover the custody procedure specific to this program. The planned build trains everyone authorized to draw a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) or open a Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) session, initially and at least annually per the CNSSI 1253 frequency for AT-3(2), on badge-reader use, intrusion alarm response and the draw, custody and return procedure that governs LRU-019 as a conditional asset, with retraining within thirty days of a significant change to the facility physical security systems. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Training records for every WS-X90 account holder are kept in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with the course and completion date, and records survive account closure for the three-year retention period. Two gaps stop the record from doing its job: there is no expiry field, so lapse has to be computed by hand from the course cadence, and the record is published as a document rather than as a machine-readable status, which is why the account enablement gates on the maintenance and provisioning paths check a date at enablement and cannot re-check it afterwards. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Training results for WS-X90 personnel are not reported to anyone; completion is recorded and not read. The planned build reports results to each person's supervisor and to the Aurora cybersecurity and privacy officials at least annually and again on discovery of a security incident or privacy breach, which are the CNSSI 1253 parameter values for AT-6, names individual failures in the maintenance, provisioning and analyst roles rather than reporting an aggregate pass rate, and files each report against the training register in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 audit and accountability policy and its implementing procedures are held as a signed record set in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), which carries the approving official, the revision number and the review date, and pushes the approved revision to the platform role dissemination list. What is missing is the procedure half: the policy was re-approved in the current annual cycle, but the procedures still describe the original 74-control audit scope and have not been rewritten for the expanded 546-control set or for the correlation and reviewer-queue behaviour now running on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018). The procedure rewrite is carried on the plan of action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Payload command records generated by the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) carry four fields beyond the AU-3 base set: the command opcode, the originating crew-station identifier, the commanded payload state and the Payload Safety Interlock state sampled at command time. LRU-010 populates each field or writes an explicit null marker rather than omitting it, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) parses the extended schema natively so an analyst sees the payload context without joining to a second source. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-4 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Audit segments written on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) are closed on a 24-hour timer or on reaching their size limit, whichever comes first, and transferred to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which is a physically separate component in a different subsystem. LRU-015 keeps the local copy until LRU-018 acknowledges receipt, so a failed transfer retries rather than losing the segment; the retry is itself recorded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Response to Audit Logging Process Failures
n: The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) reports audit partition utilisation to the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), which raises an operator warning within 60 seconds of the partition crossing 75% of its allocated capacity — the CNSSI 1253 parameter for this system — and repeats at each further 5% of consumption. The warning is written to the on-platform maintenance log as well as the operator display, so a warning raised while the crew station is unattended is still recoverable. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting
n: The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-6 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) runs the approved correlation rule set against records as they are ingested, with no operator step in the job definition, and builds a weekly reviewer queue covering the preceding seven days for the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) — the at-least-weekly cadence carried by the CNSSI 1253 parameter for AU-6. What is missing is the downstream automation: an analyst who accepts a queue item still opens the incident ticket by hand, so the review process is automated but the hand-off into incident handling is not. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) joins the on-platform audit store copied from the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) with the configuration-change history held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), keyed on actor identity and time, so a configuration change and the audit records it produced resolve to a single correlated event and an unmatched change is reported rather than dropped. The maintenance session transcript store was the third repository sitting outside that key space; it was brought inside it on 2026-10-28, so a change made during a maintenance session now resolves to the session that carried it as well as to the change record, and the analysis view can say under whose hands a change was made. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) is the single central review surface for WS-X90 audit content: an analyst reviews platform-wide activity from LRU-018 without logging in to a source component, and an LRU that misses its expected reporting interval shows as silent rather than simply absent. What is missing is live coverage of the Navigation and Timing Subsystem — records from the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) reach the central view through a batch export taken at mission close rather than the live path, so intra-mission navigation activity is not centrally reviewable until the mission ends. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design places the vulnerability scan results and the host monitoring stream produced for the Mission Computer (LRU-001) into the same analysis view on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), with a source-type column that keeps audit, scan and monitoring rows distinguishable while allowing one time-window query to return all three. Neither feed is ingested yet; the ingest adapters and the extended view schema are scheduled work and no correlated analysis across the three sources is available today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design correlates each provisioning session on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) with the facility badge entry that preceded it, so a provisioning session with no matching physical entry is raised as an exception on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018). The facility physical-access feed is owned outside the program and is not yet delivered to LRU-018; the data-source agreement, the feed format and the matching window are drafted but the correlation rule is not built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Audit Record Reduction and Report Generation
n: Audit reduction and report generation run on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) from stored queries against a read-only view of the segment store, so a report run leaves the source records byte-identical and preserves their relative order; each report header carries the query text, the requesting operator and the record count. What is missing is scope: approved report templates exist only for the original 74-control assessment scope, and templates for the expanded 546-control set are not yet written, so reporting against the new controls is done with ad-hoc queries that are not repeatable between analysts. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) indexes event type, actor identity, source LRU identifier, outcome and event timestamp, and processes, sorts and searches on any of the five. A seven-day query over the full retained platform volume returns inside 30 seconds, and sorting on event timestamp is stable so records sharing a timestamp keep a deterministic order between runs. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-8 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-9 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components
n: Every closed audit segment on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) is copied to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which sits in the Ground Support Subsystem on a different chassis from the LRUs being audited. The CNSSI 1253 parameter for this system is at least weekly; the fielded cadence is daily, and a calendar week that closes with no acknowledged copy raises a maintenance alert so the floor cannot be silently missed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Audit records and the tools that read them are integrity-protected by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003): it signs each audit segment as the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) closes it, and signs each audit tool binary before release. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) verifies both against the current platform trust anchor, quarantining a segment that fails verification rather than ingesting it and refusing execution of an unsigned or mis-signed tool. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Access by Subset of Privileged Users
n: Audit logging configuration is owned by a dedicated audit-management group of no more than three named individuals, kept disjoint from the general platform administration group. On the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) that separation is enforced by the access control policy on the audit configuration objects. What is missing is the same enforcement on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013): the platform administration group there can still alter local audit configuration, so the subset restriction holds off-platform but not on the controller itself. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design requires two distinct authenticated approvals from the audit-management group, recorded in one transaction, before any audit information — the CNSSI 1253 parameter is any audit information, not a subset — is moved or deleted on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) or the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), with a single-approval attempt failing closed and being logged as a denied action. The dual-approval transaction does not exist yet on either component; today both accept a single approval from that group. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Read-only analysis accounts reach audit content on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) through an interface that exposes no write, edit or delete verb, so read-only access is enforced by the interface surface rather than by convention. What is missing is the storage layer: the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) still exposes a maintenance write path to the segment store that is not restricted to the audit writer service identity, so a maintenance identity can in principle write to a store that should be read-only to everything but the writer. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Non-repudiation for payload actions is built from two halves. The Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) attaches a signature produced by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) to every arm and release command, covering the command, the operator identity and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) state sampled at command time, so an altered replay fails verification. LRU-003 holds the signing keys with no export path. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) verifies each signature on ingest and marks a record it cannot verify rather than discarding it. What is missing is key history: the retired-key identifier list is not yet published to LRU-018, so records signed under a rotated key verify as unknown-key and land in the unverifiable bucket even though they were validly signed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-11 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The CNSSI 1253 parameter for this enhancement is a retention of the capability to access audit records for the duration of the required retention period, which for WS-X90 means keeping the reader tooling, the record schema version and the verification key for each segment for as long as the segment itself is retained. The design places tooling and schema versions in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and the per-epoch verification keys on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015). Neither store is populated for historical epochs yet, and a segment older than the current schema version cannot today be read without an out-of-configuration tool. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of AU-12 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The system-wide audit trail is time-correlated to the platform time reference distributed by the Timing Receiver (LRU-005), which holds the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) inside the AU-8 tolerance and declares holdover with a degraded-time marker on emitted records when it cannot. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) compiles records from every reporting LRU into one trail ordered on that reference, carrying the degraded-time marker through rather than interleaving silently. The relay path was the last ordering exception and it closed on 2026-11-05, when the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) began stamping its own source time; switch-origin events are ordered on origin from that date and stay inside the tolerance while the internal segment is congested. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) exposes the logging-selection function to the audit-management group only, offering a fixed approved event-criteria set rather than free-form configuration, and every accepted or refused change is itself audited with requester, target LRU and criteria selected. Changes reach the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) within seconds. What is missing is the payload path: the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) only reads new logging configuration at a mission-mode transition, so a change can take substantially longer than 15 minutes to take effect there if the platform is mid-mission. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) captures the full command and response content of every nonlocal maintenance session, whichever maintenance account opened it, and forwards the transcript to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) at session close, including for sessions that terminate abnormally. What is missing is the second half of the control: the legal-review record required before session content may be retained and used for personnel-conduct purposes is not complete, so transcripts are currently retained for security analysis only, under a narrower retention rule than the design assumes. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Session auditing on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) is enabled by the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) as an ordered step of the authenticated boot sequence, ahead of the step that brings the maintenance port up. If the enable step fails, the boot sequence leaves the maintenance port down, so there is no window in which a maintenance session can be opened with session auditing off and no operator action is available to reorder the two steps. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has no capability for an authorized supervisor to view an in-progress maintenance session in real time. Sessions on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) are reviewable only after close, from the forwarded transcript, and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) carries no observation path. A design naming the observation path, the supervisor authorization and the technician notification is not yet approved. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design restricts release of WS-X90 audit information across an organizational boundary to a single approved coordination method bound to a named egress policy on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), with the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) recording the receiving organization, the record set released and the releasing authority for each transfer. The coordination method is drafted but not approved, the egress policies are not written, and no transfer register exists on LRU-018. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design carries the originating individual identity through unchanged in any audit record exported to a partner organization, resolving it from the platform identity binding held by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) rather than substituting a locally reassigned or per-session identifier on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018). Since no cross-organizational export path is built, the export mapping that would preserve identity does not exist and no transform has been written or reviewed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 does not share audit information with external organizations. There is no sharing-agreement record in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and no agreement check on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), because there is no release path to gate. The gap is carried on the plan of action with a named owner rather than being closed by an unused mechanism. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The assessment, authorization and continuous monitoring procedure set for SYS-WSX90 is held as signed artifacts in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), each carrying a named approver and a review date, with any artifact past a 12-month review date flagged automatically — the at-least-annual interval CNSSI 1253 sets for CA-1. Publication runs only through the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), so each revision carries the publishing operator's identity and a diff against its predecessor, and the recipient list for each revision is retained with it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CA-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Assessment independence is enforced by the access model rather than by assertion. The independent assessment team holds a dedicated assessor role on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) that can read configuration and health state but holds no permission to change a configuration item, clear an audit record or approve a remediation action, and can export the correlated record set from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) — an export that is itself recorded as an access event. The role is provisioned separately from every engineering role, and no account holds both, so nobody assesses a control they built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The programme intends to add two specialised assessments to each authorization cycle: an announced data-leakage assessment against the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) egress paths, and an unannounced malicious-user exercise against a Mission Computer (LRU-001) operator account, each producing a result that enumerates the paths or privileges exercised and what was observed rather than a completion date. Neither is scheduled yet — the assessment plan carries no specialised-assessment frequency, no announced-versus-unannounced determination has been made, and no rules of engagement exist for the malicious-user exercise. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

External exchanges are gated on agreements. Each exchange enabled in the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) policy set maps to a signed exchange agreement identifier recording interface characteristics, the impact level of the information carried, the controls each party operates and the responsible party for each, and the gateway will not enable an exchange with no agreement identifier. The Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) tactical data link agreement is signed and current. The gap is the ground-support telemetry exchange, which is running under a time-bounded interim approval while its agreement is in draft; the interim approval has an expiry recorded but the exchange is live without a signed agreement. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Inbound transfer authorization is checked at the boundary: before accepting data written into WS-X90 from an interconnected system, the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) verifies that the sending identity holds a current write authorization for the specific destination data set, and rejects and logs a transfer from an unauthorized identity or one directed at a data set outside its authorization. The reverse direction is weaker — the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) releases telemetry on link-layer identity alone, with no check against a recorded read authorization, so a receiver that has been de-authorized on paper can still be served until the link configuration is changed. That gap is carried by REQ-509. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CA-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The authorization decision for SYS-WSX90, the named authorizing official and the list of inherited common controls accepted are recorded as a signed artifact in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) surfaces the authorization reference and its expiry as part of platform status so the authorization state is visible on the platform rather than only in a file. What is outstanding is currency: the expansion of the in-scope control set from 74 to 546 controls is a significant change under the interval CNSSI 1253 sets for CA-6, and the resulting reauthorization package has not been submitted, so the recorded decision covers a narrower scope than the system now claims. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CA-7 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The independent monitoring team pulls the continuous monitoring dataset directly from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) on the agreed cadence, with no engineering-held staging step between the collector and the team, so the data they analyse is not curated by the organisation that operates the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013). Coverage is partial: independent monitoring today spans the audit, boundary and configuration families, while the contingency, maintenance and payload-interface families remain self-assessed by the engineering organisation, which is recorded in the monitoring strategy but not yet remediated. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned trend capability keeps at least 12 months of period-comparable control-monitoring outcomes in the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) and requires each monitoring-strategy revision to cite the trend that drove it — a control whose failure rate is rising, or a check whose result has been unchanged across four consecutive periods that can therefore be run less often. Today the collector retains the outcomes but not in a period-comparable form: the check identifiers were re-scoped when the control set expanded, so periods before that change cannot be compared, and no strategy revision has yet cited empirical data. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Risk monitoring is intended to be readable as three separable views for each in-scope control — effectiveness, compliance with the authorized configuration, and what changed since the previous period — with the change view built from Configuration Repository (LRU-020) commits and the other two from Security Log Collector (LRU-018) outcomes, so that a rise in risk can be attributed to a change, a drift or a degradation rather than reported as a single score. The dataset today carries a compliance result only; the effectiveness view has no defined measure per family, and the change view is not joined to repository commits. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The consistency check is designed to compare, for each control family, the approved procedure held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) against the settings the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) actually reports on each LRU, listing every divergence with the LRU, the setting and the approved value, and recording a family with no divergence as consistent for the period rather than leaving it silent. The comparison exists only as a manual spot check on two families; the machine-readable expression of the approved settings that would make it repeatable has not been authored. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Monitoring results are machine-produced and carry their own age. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) presents the current result for every in-scope control with the time it was produced, marks any result older than 24 hours as stale so an assessor cannot mistake an old pass for a current one, and raises a collection alarm when the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) feed has been silent for more than 15 minutes. The presented dataset is reproducible from the collector on demand, so no monitoring result reaches an assessor through manual assembly. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CA-8 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Independent Penetration Testing Agent or Team
n: Penetration testing of the WS-X90 external boundary at the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and of the technician session path at the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) is performed by a team holding no build or operate role on either LRU, under written rules of engagement agreed and dated before the first test activity. The report names each attempted technique and its outcome — including techniques that did not succeed — rather than listing only the findings raised, so the coverage of the test is assessable and not just its results. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No facility-directed penetration testing has been performed for WS-X90. Unannounced attempts to reach the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) enclosure or to remove or connect a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) without passing facility access control are not part of the assessment process, the assessment plan sets no frequency for them, and no authorising official has been named for such attempts. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Internal connections are governed by a register rather than by convention. The authorized internal-connection register in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) records each internal connection with its interface characteristics and the nature of the data it carries; the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) leaves a port unforwarding when the endpoint on it is absent from the register and raises a register-mismatch event, and the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) admits a payload-side connection only for a registered endpoint and terminates it when the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) leaves the armed-permissive state. Three things are missing: the sensor connections aggregated by the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) are documented in the register but not yet enforced against it, the 15-minute idle termination on payload-side connections is not implemented, and the annual review of the register has not run once since the register was expanded. Admission and termination events reported by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) are available for reconciliation but are reconciled by hand. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Configuration management direction for SYS-WSX90 lives as data, not as a shelf binder. The Configuration Repository (LRU-020) holds the CM policy and the CM procedure set as signed, version-tagged artifacts, each bound to the named Aurora CM official who owns it, and computes a review-overdue flag against the at-least-annual interval CNSSI 1253 sets for CM-1. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is the only publication endpoint, so every revision carries an operator identity, a diff against its predecessor and the dissemination list of engineering and cybersecurity role holders who received it. What is missing is coverage: the policy and the seven procedures that supported the original 74-control scope are current and signed, but the procedures for the configuration management enhancements the expanded set introduced — automated change prohibition, automated security response, information location and signed components — are drafted and unsigned, so four of the eleven required procedures show as review-overdue in the repository today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Automation Support for Accuracy and Currency
n: Baseline currency is machine-maintained on the platform side and manual on the ground side. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) pushes each observed change of part number, firmware version or configuration set to the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) inside a 15-minute window, and LRU-020 marks the affected baseline record stale until the push is reconciled, recording the prior value alongside the observed one. The gap is scope: LRU-013 observes the platform LRUs it manages directly, but the Ground Support Subsystem items — the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) and the repository host itself — are still reconciled by a technician on a weekly cadence, so their baseline records can sit stale for up to seven days. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Rollback depth is held at three: the current approved baseline plus at least two prior approved versions, matching the retention CNSSI 1253 sets for CM-2(3). The Configuration Repository (LRU-020) keeps each retained version with its original approval signature and re-verifies those signatures on a weekly integrity sweep, reporting a retention integrity fault rather than quietly dropping a version that no longer verifies. The Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) can stage and apply any retained version as a rollback using repository content alone, which is what makes the retention meaningful — the rollback path was exercised in the last integration campaign and completed without reaching outside LRU-020 for a missing artifact. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Configure Systems and Components for High-risk Areas
n: The travel configuration for the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is designed and not yet built. The intent is a reduced image that carries no mission data, no provisioning key material and no cached maintenance credentials, issued and returned through a recorded transaction on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), with mandatory re-imaging and re-enrolment before LRU-019 may open a maintenance session again. The image definition and the issue/return record schema are drafted; the enforcement that prevents a returned laptop from opening a session before re-enrolment is not built, and today the return step is a procedural instruction rather than a technical gate. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Automated Documentation, Notification, and Prohibition of Changes
n: Change automation runs in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020): every proposed change gets a record, the record is routed to its named approval authorities, and the release of the change artifact for staging is refused until the required approvals are present — the prohibition is enforced by the repository, not by discipline. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) refuses any configuration set that arrives without a released change record identifier, which closes the second path onto the platform. Two of the six behaviours the enhancement asks for are weak: the aging highlight for records left undecided beyond 10 working days is computed but only surfaced in a weekly report rather than pushed to the approvers, and completion notification reaches the originator but not yet the affected engineering lead. Both are carried against REQ-563. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Testing, Validation, and Documentation of Changes
n: No WS-X90 change reaches an operational platform without a recorded test and validation. The Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) will accept a change package for application only when the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) holds three things against that change record: a completed test result, a validation statement naming the specific security controls examined, and the identity of the engineer who signed it. A package presented with any of the three missing is held in the staging area and reported as an incomplete record, which is the mechanism that keeps the requirement from degrading into a checkbox — the validation statement has to name controls, and a statement that merely asserts compliance is rejected at review. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 configuration control board exists and meets, but the cybersecurity representative currently attends in an advisory capacity rather than as the voting member CNSSI 1253 directs for CM-3(4). The planned change amends the board charter to designate the representative and a named alternate as voting members, and extends the decision record the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) writes so that the representative's vote is a required field on every board decision, with dissent carried into the outcome text rather than summarised away. Neither the charter amendment nor the decision-record change has been made. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Automatic response to an out-of-process baseline change is designed around the two components that already hold platform state. The Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) both detect a baseline value with no released change record today, and both raise it; what they do not yet do is act on it. The planned build drives the affected function to its restricted state, refuses the next mission-enable transition and raises a priority event to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) within 60 seconds, with return to normal gated on an approved change record or a recorded override. Because availability is categorised moderate, the restricted state is scoped to the affected function rather than a whole-platform halt. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every cryptographic mechanism WS-X90 depends on is a configuration item, which is what CNSSI 1253 asks for when it scopes CM-3(6) to all controls that rely on cryptography. The algorithm suites, key strengths, certificate trust anchors and module firmware versions of the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) are registered in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), and each crypto-dependent control in the tailored set resolves to at least one of those items. Changing any of them is a configuration change with a board decision behind it — there is no operational console path to set an algorithm suite or add a trust anchor, and an attempt is refused and logged. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Applied changes are reviewed against a monthly cadence, the interval CNSSI 1253 sets for a high-integrity system under CM-3(7), by reconciling the change records in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) against the change-related events retained by the Security Log Collector (LRU-018). The reconciliation reports two exception classes separately: applied-without-record and record-without-applied. Three monthly reviews are complete. The event-driven half is weaker — a post-incident review was run after the August integration incident, but there is no automatic trigger that opens a review once a planned change campaign completes, so that leg currently depends on the engineer remembering. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Blocking configuration change during exercises and real-world operations — the circumstance CNSSI 1253 names for CM-3(8) — is designed as two independent refusals so that neither is a single point of bypass. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) will refuse to apply any configuration change while the platform reports an operational or exercise state, and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) will independently refuse an interlock parameter change in those states even when the request carries a valid change record. Requests arriving in a blocked state are queued with the blocking state recorded rather than discarded. The platform state signal exists; neither refusal is implemented yet. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-4 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The ground test rig driven from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is a separate environment from the operational platform and every change package is applied there first, with the analysis record filed against the change in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). Two things are short of the intent. The analysis record reports a single verdict rather than the four separate headings — defect, weakness, incompatibility and suspected malicious content — that would let an assessor see what was actually looked for; and the rig does not yet include a Payload Interface Subsystem representative, so payload-affecting changes are analysed against a simulated interface and the record does not state that limitation. Both gaps are carried against REQ-570. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Post-change verification is wired to the change record: the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) reads the controls the record marks as impacted, runs the verification set associated with each and reports results to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), holding the platform out of mission-ready state until every verification in the set reports. The limitation is coverage of the verification library — verification sets exist for 41 of the controls in the expanded set, concentrated in AC, AU, CM and SI, so a change marked as impacting a control with no verification set is currently recorded as unverifiable and released on an engineering judgement rather than a test. Building out the remaining sets is the open work behind REQ-571. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Automated Access Enforcement and Audit Records
n: Change access is enforced at two points and audited at both. The Configuration Repository (LRU-020) checks every write against the authorised change role list before it touches a baseline, a change record or a release artifact, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) applies the same list to change actions that arrive through a maintenance session, so there is no second path that reaches a released artifact without passing an enforcement point. Every decision, permit and deny alike, produces an audit record carrying actor identity, object and decision, forwarded to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) — the deny records matter more than the permits here, because they are what shows the enforcement is live rather than nominal. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Privilege Limitation for Production and Operation
n: Privilege to change components on the operational platform is issued through the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and honoured by the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), and the operational change role is held separately from the development role. The annual re-evaluation CNSSI 1253 requires under CM-5(5) has been performed once and withdrew two dormant holders. Two weaknesses remain: three integration engineers hold both the development and the operational change role under an exception that has no expiry date, and the re-evaluation is currently a spreadsheet exercise against an exported list rather than a review inside the tool that grants the privilege, so the record and the grant can drift between reviews. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The mission software library on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) accepts content from exactly one identity — the release pipeline identity issued by the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) — and from no interactive account, administrative accounts included. Enforcement sits at the filesystem enforcement point rather than in the application, so an attempted write from any other identity is refused before it reaches library contents and is reported as a library privilege violation naming the attempting identity. This is the narrower of the two library protections on the platform: it constrains who may write, while the execution policy constrains what may run. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-6 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Configuration settings are applied and verified by machine across the security-relevant component set — at minimum all cybersecurity and cybersecurity-enabled components, the scope CNSSI 1253 gives CM-6(1). The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) pushes the approved setting set and then reads it back at every bring-up and at least once in any 24-hour period of sustained operation, reporting each deviation as a named setting rather than a count. The scope deliberately reaches into the Navigation & Timing Subsystem: the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) integrity-check thresholds and the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) holdover and source-authentication settings are verified on the same cycle as the mission compute settings, because a silently loosened navigation threshold is an integrity failure, not a tuning choice. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Response to an unauthorised setting change is automatic restoration plus a named event: the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) writes back the approved value, marks the affected function as reverted, and raises an event to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) carrying the setting, the observed value and the restored value. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004) case is handled specially and correctly — a revert is deferred to a navigation solution handover boundary so the revert never drops the solution mid-computation, and the deferral is recorded with its duration. What is missing is the equivalent handling for the Communications Subsystem: a revert on the Protected Network Gateway currently resets the affected session, which is why REQ-576 remains partially satisfied.
