This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-7 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The least-functionality review runs on two fronts. Inside the platform, the functions, software and services on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) are reviewed against the approved function list in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) at least annually and after a change or incident, the trigger set CNSSI 1253 gives for CM-7(1); anything unnecessary or nonsecure is disabled or removed, and anything retained carries a written justification and a review date. Outward, the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007), the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) and the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) are constrained to the approved external interface set. The shortfall is on the sensor interface: LRU-006 still exposes two vendor diagnostic services that are enabled in the shipped configuration with no approved entry, and disabling them is blocked on a vendor firmware release. That is the open item behind REQ-578. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Execution prevention is anchored in measurement, not in file permissions. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) computes the measurement of every image at load and refuses it if that measurement is absent from the approved program set anchored by the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002); the refusal happens at load, so an unapproved binary never reaches an executing state rather than being killed after start. The refusal record names the image path and the computed measurement, and the same path is enforced in maintenance mode — a mode switch does not relax the policy, which was the specific weakness the design set out to avoid. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Registration compliance for ports, protocols and services is currently a paper reconciliation performed at release review. The planned build gives every service exposed through the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) a registration identifier recorded against its configuration item in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), and runs an automated reconciliation of the gateway configuration against that register before each release, reporting unregistered services and port mismatches as separate exception classes with a named owner and a target date. The register schema is agreed; the reconciliation is not built and no gateway service carries a registration identifier in the repository yet. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 runs deny-all, permit-by-exception. The authorised software list in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) is the only permit source for the Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), and each entry names the program, its measurement and the mission function it supports — the third field is what makes the annual review CNSSI 1253 requires under CM-7(5) more than a rubber stamp, because an entry with no current mission function is removed rather than carried forward. The most recent review removed four entries on that basis, two of them development-era diagnostic utilities that had survived three baselines. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No supplier warranty or source-availability determination is recorded against WS-X90 software configuration items, and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) applies no publication check for binary-only content. The control is unimplemented; the determination field and the authorising-official exception record are scoped against REQ-582 and not yet built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Prohibiting The Use of Unauthorized Hardware
n: The authorised hardware list is maintained by the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) with each entry tied to a platform build, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) enforces it on the maintenance port - an unlisted device is refused a session and reported. The Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) was the weaker half until 2026-11-11, when the four of its twelve ports still running firmware that predated the enforcement build were reflashed; all twelve now refuse an unlisted device a data path and report it inside the thirty-second bound, instead of four of them raising the report while the traffic continued. The annual list review CNSSI 1253 sets for CM-7(9) has been completed once. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-8 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The inventory update is part of the maintenance action rather than a follow-up to it. A maintenance action that installs, removes or replaces an LRU cannot be closed until the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) has written the inventory delta — part number, serial number, firmware version and slot, for both the removed and the installed unit — to the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and had it accepted. An action closed without an accepted delta stays open and is reported to the maintenance supervisor, which is what stops the inventory decaying between formal audits. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Inventory currency is measured rather than assumed. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) polls the platform for installed component identity at least once per operating day and publishes the result to the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), which computes an inventory currency figure — the proportion of records confirmed by an automated observation inside 24 hours — and forwards it to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) so the trend is visible alongside the security event stream. Records outside the window are listed individually with the age of their last confirmation instead of being absorbed into a percentage, and no record is marked confirmed on a manual entry alone. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Detection of unauthorised components is continuous rather than scheduled, which is the frequency CNSSI 1253 sets for CM-8(3). On the software and firmware side the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) and the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) compare observed measurements against the approved baseline as they change, isolate the affected function from the mission network and notify the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) inside 5 minutes. On the hardware side the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) quarantines a port presenting an unlisted device and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) refuses traffic sourced from a quarantined segment. Two gaps remain: the firmware comparison does not yet cover the Payload Interface Subsystem controllers, whose measurements are read only at bring-up, and switch quarantine is enforcement-capable on eight of twelve ports. Both are tracked against REQ-586 and REQ-587. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Component records in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) carry an accountability field holding the position or role responsible for administering the component — at minimum a position or role, as CNSSI 1253 scopes CM-8(4) — drawn from the four engineering roles this programme uses, and the field holds a role rather than a personal name so it does not decay when staff move. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) refuses a new component record with the field empty. The gap is historical: 6 of the 20 component records were created before the field was mandatory and still carry an inherited default of Platform Lead that has not been confirmed against the current engineering assignment. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 configuration management plan is itself a configuration item: signed, version-tagged and held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with recorded programme and cybersecurity approvals, mirrored to the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) so a recovery does not lose it, and readable only by holders of a configuration management role, with refused reads logged. The plan defines the configuration item classes and the identification process across the lifecycle. What is not current is the content: the plan still describes the original 74-control scope and does not yet address the configuration item classes the expanded set introduces — cryptographic mechanism items under CM-3(6), signed component certificate sets under CM-14, and information location records under CM-12. The revision is drafted and awaiting board approval. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-10 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Open-source admission is gated on three recorded facts per component and version — the licence determination, the upstream provenance reference and the named reviewing engineer — held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), with a versioned prohibited licence list carrying its own owner. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) refuses to publish a build whose bill of materials contains a component with a prohibited licence. The incomplete half is provenance: licence determinations are recorded for every open-source entry in the current bill of materials, but upstream provenance references are recorded for roughly two thirds, mostly missing on transitively pulled build-time dependencies, and the publication check does not yet fail a build for a missing provenance reference. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CM-11 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Software installation onto the Mission Computer (LRU-001) requires a maintenance session that has been explicitly elevated to installation privilege for a bounded period; an ordinary session from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) cannot trigger an installation at all. Elevation is requested per action rather than per session, expires automatically at the end of its window with no operator step, and is recorded with the requesting identity, the elevation window and the installed package identifier — so an installation is always attributable to a person and a time-boxed grant rather than to a standing privilege. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The information location record in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) maps each class of protected WS-X90 information to the components that process and store it and to the roles and accounts that can reach it on each — principally the Mission Computer (LRU-001) working set and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) at-rest set — and a relocation is captured as a dated location-change record with a reason, so the map is maintained rather than a design-time snapshot. The payload side is thinner: the retention points for telemetry collected by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) and relayed through the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) are documented for the primary buffers but not for the diagnostic ring buffer LRU-012 holds during fault capture, and no release gate yet refuses a change that introduces a new retention point. Both are open against REQ-593. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Automated Tools to Support Information Location
n: Automated discovery of protected information types is designed to run inside the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which already holds the exported platform data sets, and to report each occurrence found on a component not recorded as holding that information type to the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) as an information location exception naming component, information type and detection basis. Discovery is to be scheduled rather than on-request, and an exception closes only on a recorded relocation, removal or corrected location record. The information type definitions exist; the discovery capability and the exception record are not built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Signature verification for any software and firmware component — the scope CNSSI 1253 sets for CM-14 — is enforced at two independent points. At boot, the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) verifies each firmware component in the chain against the approved certificate set held in the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and halts the affected LRU in its recovery state on failure; there is no operational configuration setting that disables the check. Before that, the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) verifies every component inside an update package at staging and rejects the whole package if one component fails, rather than staging the verifiable subset, with the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) recording the certificate identity that verified each accepted component so provenance is reconstructible after the fact. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Contingency planning direction for SYS-WSX90 is not a shelf document: the policy and the recovery procedure set are held as signed, version-tagged artifacts in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), which flags any artifact whose recorded review date passes 12 months and refuses an unsigned revision. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is the only publication path, so every revision carries an operator identity, a diff against its predecessor and the distribution list of contingency role holders who received it. Review runs on the at-least-annual interval CNSSI 1253 sets for CP-1. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CP-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The contingency plan and the incident response plan are coupled at the trigger rather than at the document. When the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) declares a platform state matching a contingency activation trigger, it emits one correlated event carrying both plan references, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) retains that correlation so an after-action review reads one timeline. What is missing is breadth: the trigger table cross-references the incident response plan for every trigger, but the depot supply and maintenance continuity plans are cross-referenced for only four of nine triggers, and the remaining five are carried as an open action against REQ-482. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design intent is that the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) restores the approved mission application baseline onto the Mission Computer (LRU-001) and returns the essential mission functions named in the contingency plan to service inside the plan's four-hour objective, with non-essential functions explicitly deferred and reported rather than counted. Nothing is built yet: the essential-function list has been drafted but not baselined, the per-function self-test set that would measure resumption does not exist, and no timed restoration exercise has been run. Consistent with the moderate availability categorisation, the intended approach is a measured staged restoration, not a hot standby. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The critical asset list is generated, not maintained. Each LRU baseline record in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) carries a mission-essential designation with a recorded rationale, and the list is produced by querying those designations, so a baseline commit that adds, removes or re-scopes an LRU changes the list in the same commit and cannot drift from it. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) carry the designation because loss of either ends the position and timing function on which the essential mission functions depend. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Contingency training is enforced by the platform rather than tracked on a spreadsheet. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) reads the contingency-role training record bound to the technician's Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) credential and refuses to open a recovery-role session when that record is absent, older than 12 months, or dated more than 10 working days after the technician assumed the role — the intervals CNSSI 1253 sets for CP-3. The gap is population: the gate is enforced for depot technicians, while field maintenance sessions still open on a supervisor override that records the override but does not check training currency. Closing that override is tracked against REQ-485. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The contingency plan is exercised semi-annually by restoring a representative platform article from a sealed Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) backup set through the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016), with the exercise recorded as failed if any restored partition fails integrity or the measured duration exceeds the plan's four-hour objective. Two tabletop reviews and one partial restore have been completed. What is missing is the full-article exercise: the most recent run restored the mission software partition only, because the flight-configuration article was not released for test, so the platform management and payload interface partitions have never been restored end to end and the measured duration covers a partial scope. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The intent is one schedule and one after-action review: the contingency plan test, the incident response exercise and the maintenance continuity rehearsal run as a single joint activity, with the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) retaining one correlated event set built from Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) state changes rather than three unlinked sets. Today the three activities are scheduled by different owners and reviewed separately. The joint schedule, the named related-plan owners and the correlation key that would tie the three event sets together are all still to be established. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Backup sets produced from the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and the signed baselines held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) are stored at a designated Aurora alternate facility under a written storage and retrieval agreement naming the custodian, the release approver and a maximum retrieval time, and one retrieval rehearsal has returned a usable backup set and a usable baseline set inside that time. The equivalence obligation is not met: the alternate facility's access approval and handling rules have been collected but not yet assessed line by line against the primary facility's rules, so the claim that the alternate provides equivalent controls is asserted rather than demonstrated. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The alternate facility holding the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) replica is recorded in the contingency plan with its separation distance from the primary facility, its independent utility feed and its own site access control, and each replica set is verified as hash-identical to the primary before it counts as the alternate. What is incomplete is the decorrelation argument: the plan names the hazards separation is intended to address, but the regional-event analysis — shared transport corridor and shared regional power provider — has not been finished, so a residual shared-threat exposure is neither quantified nor formally accepted. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned approach lists, for each access route to the alternate facility, the obstacle that would delay retrieval of Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) backup media during an area-wide disruption, with a named mitigation and a responsible role, and walks the retrieval sequence through to standing up the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) instance at that facility. Nothing has been written down yet: no obstacle list exists, the media release authorisation names an organisation rather than a role, and no retrieval walkthrough has been rehearsed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The intended alternate processing arrangement is a written agreement making a second Aurora integration facility available to host a Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) build and a Mission Computer (LRU-001) integration article, sufficient to resume the mission-support operations the contingency plan names within its five working-day transfer objective. Because WS-X90 is categorised A:moderate, the design is a staged transfer with equipment delivered on call — not a continuously warm standby, and the plan says so rather than implying capability the programme does not fund. The agreement is in negotiation, the equipment list is drafted but carries no delivery commitment, and no transfer has been rehearsed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The candidate alternate processing facility is separated from the primary integration site and, on the survey completed to date, draws its power and network entry from different providers and runs its own badge system. The record that would make this a control rather than a fact — the separation entry in the contingency plan, the threat set the separation is intended to decorrelate, and a signed confirmation of the independent utility and network entries — has not been produced, so the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) alternate build is still nominated rather than assured. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No accessibility analysis exists for the alternate processing facility. The obstacles that would prevent staff and equipment from reaching it during an area-wide disruption, and the mitigations for each, have not been identified, so the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) alternate build is nominated in the plan without any assurance it could be reached. This is tracked as an open gap. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The draft agreement for the alternate processing facility carries no priority-of-service provision, so the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) build could be queued behind other tenants of the same facility with no contractual basis to object. No clause referencing the contingency plan's recovery time objective has been proposed to the facility owner. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The intended alternate telecommunications design uses the two bearers the platform already carries: the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) takes the mission data operations the contingency plan names as essential when the primary ground bearer is lost, reaching a 30-minute resumption objective, while the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) detects bearer loss within 60 seconds and re-establishes the protected tunnel over the alternate bearer under an identical policy set. Neither behaviour is fielded: the essential-operations list is not baselined, bearer-loss detection is manual today, and no failover has been timed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The intent is that both the primary and the alternate telecommunications service agreements supporting the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) carry priority-of-service provisions tied to the recovery time objective in the contingency plan, and that the agreement file records, for each common-carrier service, either a submitted national security emergency preparedness priority request reference or the reason the service is out of scope. Today neither agreement contains such a clause and no priority request has been submitted or ruled out in writing. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Carrier-side disjointness has been established and demonstrated: the primary and alternate services traverse different transmission lines and different carrier points of presence, and a path trace built from live configuration rather than from a drawing shows no shared carrier element between the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) path and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) path. On-platform the two paths still converge — both transit the same port group on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009), which is the single point of failure the control is meant to remove. Re-homing the radio path onto a separate port group is the open item behind REQ-498. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CP-9 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Backup reliability is verified rather than assumed. At least monthly — the interval CNSSI 1253 sets for CP-9(1) — the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) recomputes the hash tree of every backup set held on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and restores at least one randomly selected partition to a scratch volume, recording which partition was chosen and its integrity result. A verification that fails, or that has not run within 31 days of its predecessor, raises a maintenance alert that cannot be cleared without a subsequent passing verification and that survives a controller restart. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every backup set sealed on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) is transferred to the alternate storage facility, and the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) records the transfer with the set identifier, the sealing hash and the receiving custodian's confirmed hash, so a mismatch is visible on receipt. The transfer itself is a signed-media courier run staged from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), which meets the five working-day objective in practice but is not measured against it automatically: no check compares elapsed time from sealing to recorded receipt, so a missed run is found at the next audit rather than reported as a recovery-point gap when it happens. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Backup material is protected as a unit and its keys never leave hardware. The Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) encrypts and integrity-tags a backup set as a whole before it will mark the set sealed, and refuses to seal a set on which either operation was suppressed; a raw read of the backup partition yields no recoverable configuration, audit or key-shadow content. The wrapping and integrity keys are generated and used inside the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), which serves a backup wrap or unwrap only to the storage role identity that seals and opens backup sets and rejects and logs the request under any other identity, including maintenance roles. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of CP-10 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Recovery is transactional on both of the platform's transaction-shaped paths. The Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) journals each staged update or configuration transaction with a commit record, discards a partial transaction on interruption, and marks a transaction complete only when the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) attests that the image the platform actually booted matches the intended image. On the payload side the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) journals each command with its authorization reference and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) state at issue, and replays the journal after a reset before accepting a new command. Two gaps remain: the platform management configuration partition still requires a technician to select the rollback point rather than rolling back automatically, and the reconstructed payload state reported by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) is compared with observed behaviour by hand. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
Planned: The tactical data radio carries a fallback protocol when the primary bearer is denied.
The mission computer enters restricted safe mode on any failed partition integrity check.
n2: Planned: A failed integrity check drops the mission computer into a restricted safe mode.

n: Planned: An alternate authentication path exists for flightline maintenance when the primary is unavailable.

The WS-X90 identification and authentication policy and its procedure set are not shelf documents: both are held as signed, version-tagged artifacts in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), which computes a review-overdue flag once an artifact passes 12 months since its recorded review and refuses to publish an unsigned revision. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is the only publication path, so each revision carries the approving official, a diff against its predecessor and the distribution list of cybersecurity and ground support role holders who received it. Review runs on the at-least-annual interval CNSSI 1253 sets for IA-1, and the designated official for the IA policy is the System Security Engineer. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of IA-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Privileged access to WS-X90 runs through two enforcement points. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) opens no administrative session and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) dispatches no maintenance command until both factors verify: a hardware credential whose private key is generated inside and never leaves the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), and an operator PIN entered at the endpoint. There is no reduced-privilege fallback session, so a single-factor attempt ends at refusal rather than at a degraded grant, and every refusal reaches the security log with the credential serial but not the PIN. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Non-privileged operator access on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) requires a hardware credential plus PIN on every path, and the workstation build exposes no password-only authentication method. The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) enforces the same pair when it is attached to the ground support network. What is missing is the disconnected case: when LRU-019 operates on the flightline with no path to the identity service, a local password-only logon remains available as an availability concession, and that path is the open gap. Closing it needs the offline credential verifier that is being built for the LRU-019 baseline, tracked in the POA and M for this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 keeps two shared role accounts, a flightline maintenance role on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and a provisioning operator role on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017). On LRU-014 the technician authenticates individually first and the gateway stamps that individual identity onto every action taken under the shared role, so no audit record resolves to the role name alone. LRU-017 authenticates the individual but does not yet propagate the identity into records written by the provisioning batch tooling, which still attributes to the role account. The fix is a change to the batch tool session context and is the open half of this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The separate-device factor is a hardware token issued to each technician; its authentication key lives inside a certified hardware boundary on the token, and the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) validates the token attestation before a session opens on either endpoint. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) applies this on its local console, its network path and its remote support path, and terminates the session within 30 seconds of token removal. The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) applies it on the network and remote paths only; its local console still accepts a factor pair that both originate on the laptop, so the scope CNSSI 1253 sets for IA-2(6), local, network and remote access for privileged and non-privileged accounts alike, is not yet fully met. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Replay resistance on the communications path is structural rather than procedural. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) issues a single-use nonce at the start of each authentication and binds it into the session key derivation, so a captured exchange re-sent later derives no usable key and is refused under a distinct replay-detected reason code. The Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) applies the same construction to link authentication and records the nonce in its sortie session log, where each value appears exactly once. Coverage exceeds the privileged-accounts-at-a-minimum level CNSSI 1253 sets for IA-2(8): every account type on both LRUs is covered because the mechanism is in the protocol, not in an account policy. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

PIV acceptance is a ground support capability on WS-X90. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) reads a PIV-compliant credential, chains the certificate up to a trust anchor on the WS-X90 accepted list and checks revocation status before binding an operator account, and refuses a credential whose status cannot be determined rather than accepting it with a warning. The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) reads the credential and chains it to an anchor but relies on the workstation for revocation data, so when the laptop is used disconnected it is operating on a revocation snapshot rather than a live check. Making the laptop enforce the same staleness refusal is the open work. Airborne LRUs do not read PIV credentials and are out of scope for this enhancement. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of IA-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Bidirectional device authentication is in place on the internal data path and partly in place on the sensor path. The Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) and each attached device complete a mutual certificate exchange before the port leaves the quarantine VLAN, with the device credential released by the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) only after a successful measured boot, and the Mission Computer (LRU-001) drops mission traffic from any port not in the authenticated state. On the navigation side the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) authenticates mutually with the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) at power-on, but the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) currently authenticates in one direction only, so LRU-004 proves itself to the receiver without the receiver proving itself back on every reconnection. The mutual exchange for the timing link is the open item. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of IA-4 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Individual identifiers on WS-X90 carry an affiliation attribute drawn from an approved set of government civilian, military, prime contractor, subcontractor and foreign national. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) collects the attribute at registration and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) stores it on the identifier record and stamps it onto audit records the account produces. Two gaps remain: the interactive registration path fails closed on a missing attribute but the bulk import path used for the initial ground support roster does not, and roughly 30 identifiers imported before the check was added still carry a legacy unspecified value. A reconciliation sweep and the import-path check are the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 keeps one attribute store, not a set of per-LRU copies. Identifier, affiliation, credential binding, issuing authority and status for every user, device and service live in a protected region of the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015). The only writer is the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) over an authenticated channel, and each accepted write appends an immutable revision record naming the writer, the timestamp and the prior value, so attribute history is reconstructible without depending on the audit pipeline. Read access is granted to the identity service principal alone; provisioning tooling queries through that service rather than reading the region. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of IA-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Passwords remain in use on WS-X90 only as the knowledge factor inside multi-factor authentication, and they are handled in two places. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) holds the commonly used, expected and compromised password list and screens every creation and change made through the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), rejecting a match without naming the entry. The Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) receives the candidate over a cryptographically protected channel and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) holds only a salted keyed-hash derivation, with the derivation key resident in LRU-003. The composition rule CNSSI 1253 sets for IA-5(1)(h), a case-sensitive 12-character mix with at least one uppercase, lowercase, numeric and special character and at least 50 percent of characters changed on update, is enforced at creation. Two gaps stand: the list refresh has been running on an ad hoc cadence rather than the at-least-quarterly interval the parameter sets, and the automated strength-assistance tool for operators has not been fielded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Public key authentication is the primary mechanism on WS-X90 and the private key never leaves hardware: the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) generates each authentication key as a non-exportable object bound to a single subject, refuses export requests and audits them. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) performs the relying-party half, chaining the certificate up to a trust anchor on the WS-X90 accepted list and checking status against a locally cached revocation set. That cache is refreshed whenever an external link is available, which suits a system whose availability category is moderate and which spends long periods disconnected; a cache older than 7 days is declared stale and the session is refused rather than accepted on an assumption. The authenticated identity is mapped to a single account, never to a group. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 is categorised confidentiality high, so every authenticator that can reach mission data is protected at that level with no per-credential downgrade. Authenticator material exists in exactly two places: inside the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) hardware boundary, or in the encrypted credential region of the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) whose key is itself held in LRU-003. The access control list on that region names only the identity service principal, and mission or provisioning software reaches credentials through the service interface rather than the storage path, so a memory or storage image taken from the Mission Computer or the Provisioning Workstation yields no authenticator material. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Configuration Repository (LRU-020) runs a credential-pattern scan across every artifact submitted for publication and refuses to publish one that flags, and the Update and Recovery Controller (LRU-016) refuses to stage a package that carries no passing scan verdict, so the normal software path cannot deliver an embedded unencrypted authenticator. The gap is coverage rather than mechanism: the scan rules were written for compiled images and configuration files and do not yet parse the payload command script format executed by the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010), so those scripts are published on the strength of a manual review. A script-aware rule set is in development and is the open item for this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design is an acknowledgement gate rather than a technical control, because WS-X90 cannot see the other systems on which a ground support user holds accounts. At each credential set the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) will present the reuse prohibition CNSSI 1253 sets for IA-5(8), that the same password must not be reused across domains of differing classification levels, across more than one domain of a single classification level, or across more than one privilege level, and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) will hold the dated acknowledgement on the account record and block the credential-set workflow until it is present. Neither the prompt nor the account record field has been built; both are scheduled with the ground support tooling drop. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Disconnected flightline work needs a cached authenticator, so WS-X90 bounds how long one stays usable. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) expires a cached authenticator 12 hours after the last successful online verification, holds the expiry timer in monotonic form so a power cycle does not reset it, and refuses the session afterwards until the endpoint reconnects to the identity service. The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) applies the same 12-hour bound but stores the timer in a form that a full power cycle resets, so a technician can extend a cached credential past its intended life by rebooting. Moving the laptop timer onto the trusted counter is the open item. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Managing Content of PKI Trust Stores
n: One signed trust store manifest in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) is the sole authority for the anchors any WS-X90 LRU may load, naming each anchor with its purpose and expiry. The Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) reports the digest of its installed trust store at power-on and a mismatch raises a configuration deviation. The Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) reports its digest only during a maintenance download rather than at power-on, so a trust store drift on that unit can go unnoticed until the next maintenance cycle. Bringing LRU-012 onto power-on reporting is the open item; the distribution of new manifests to both units also remains a manual maintenance action rather than an automated push. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: In-person or Trusted External Party Authenticator Issuance
n: The intended process issues every privileged-role hardware authenticator in person at the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), before the designated registration authority, with the issuing officer identity and the authorising government sponsor recorded against the credential serial number before activation. Today credentials are issued in person by local practice but the sponsor authorisation is captured on a separate form and is not bound to the serial number in the provisioning record, so the binding cannot be verified from the system. The work is procedural documentation plus a provisioning record field, scheduled with the identity proofing drop. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Authentication feedback is suppressed at both ground support endpoints. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) mask PIN and password entry on every surface including the recovery console, keep the entered characters out of logs, crash dumps and diagnostic buffers by never copying them out of the credential input buffer, and return one generic failure message whether the identifier or the authenticator was wrong. The two failure paths were also equalised in timing to within 50 milliseconds so response latency does not become the disclosure channel the masked display closes. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Access to the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) is role-bound, not merely session-bound. An operator or service authenticates to the module and is bound to a defined module role before any keyed operation is accepted, a keyed request arriving before role authentication returns a module status refusal, and a transition between roles requires a fresh authentication rather than inheriting the earlier one. The Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) participates by refusing a key-wrapping request that does not carry a valid LRU-003 role binding, so the storage module cannot be used as a path around the module role check. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of IA-8 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Acceptance of PIV Credentials from Other Agencies
n: Other-agency technician support is an anticipated case for WS-X90 rather than a current one. The design has the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) accept the visiting agency PIV credential, verify it electronically against the issuing agency trust anchor and revocation source captured as part of the support authorisation, and bind it to a non-organisational account whose expiry equals the authorisation end date with no in-place extension. Nothing is built: the workstation reads only anchors from the WS-X90 trust store manifest today, and the non-organisational account type does not exist in the account model. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A list of external authenticators approved for non-organisational access to WS-X90 support interfaces is held as a signed artifact in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with type, assurance level, approver and approval date per entry. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) enforces the list on the support interface and refuses an unlisted authenticator type. The gap is currency and completeness: the list was populated from the initial support agreements and has no scheduled review, and the gateway configuration pins a list revision rather than tracking the current one, so an approval added in the repository does not reach enforcement until a configuration change is pushed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The intent is that non-organisational identity handling on WS-X90 conforms to one recorded identity management profile, held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and enforced by the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), which would reject an external identity assertion whose attribute set, binding method or assurance level does not match the profile revision in force. The profile has not been selected or written, and LRU-013 has no external assertion path in the current build, so this is design only. Selection is being held until the external authenticator list under IA-8(2) settles, because the two constrain each other. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 authenticates services, not just the boxes hosting them. Each mission service holds a per-service certificate whose subject names both the service and its hosting LRU, issued during provisioning and renewed at each software baseline. The service mesh on the Mission Computer (LRU-001), the telemetry publisher on the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) and the navigation solution service on the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) all present that certificate on connection and refuse a peer that offers only a device credential or a certificate whose subject does not match the hosting LRU inventory entry. The effect is that a compromised but authenticated device still cannot impersonate a service it does not host. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No adaptive authentication capability exists on WS-X90. The circumstance detection that would drive it, a maintenance session opening outside the authorised support window or from a ground network address not on the approved list, is within reach of the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) but is not implemented, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) has no supplemental factor prompt to raise. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Re-authentication is enforced at the two points where authorisation would otherwise be inherited across a change of context. On the ground support side the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) demands the full factor set again before any privilege escalation, before any maintenance role reassignment, and after 30 minutes of session inactivity, and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) discards its session key at each of those triggers so a resumed session cannot carry the earlier grant. On the payload side the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) requires a two-person re-authentication completed within the preceding 5 minutes before it releases an arming state to the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010), rejects an arming command backed by an older authentication, and reverts to the safe state when a subsequent arming command arrives without a renewed authentication. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Identity proofing for WS-X90 accounts runs at the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) before an account is enabled: the registration authority proofs the applicant, resolves them to a single named individual with no shared or role-only registration accepted, and records the identity evidence collected against the account. Two things are short of the intent. The assurance level required per role is documented in the ground support handbook rather than held as a controlled artifact the workstation can enforce, so the level applied depends on the registration authority reading it correctly, and the record captures collection and validation but treats verification as an implicit step with no separate outcome field. Both are addressed by the identity proofing drop that also carries IA-12(3). This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No WS-X90 account reaches the enabled state without a named sponsor. A registration submitted at the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) sits in a pending state until a government sponsor or supervisor authorises it, and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) refuses to enable an account whose authorisation record is absent or names the applicant as their own sponsor. The record naming the sponsor, the role requested and the date is retained with the account for its whole life, including after the account is disabled, so a later review can reconstruct who vouched for a privilege that has since been removed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The registration authority at the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) requires physical identity evidence at registration and records the type, issuer and reference for each item, deliberately storing no document image so the registration store never becomes a collection of scanned credentials. The shortfall is enforcement of the minimum: the workflow accepts a registration with a single evidence item, so the one photo credential plus one supporting document minimum currently rests on registration authority discipline rather than on the tool. Adding the two-item minimum check is the open work for this enhancement. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned approach fixes two approved methods for identity evidence, issuer or authoritative-source confirmation for validation and a biometric comparison against the presented credential for verification, and has the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) record the method and outcome per evidence item, holding a registration out of the enabled state when either returns an inconclusive outcome. Neither method is in use today: validation is a visual inspection by the registration authority and verification is not separately recorded, so the record fields, the approved method artifact and the biometric comparison step all remain to be built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Privileged-role applicants are proofed with the applicant physically present before the designated registration authority at the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), and that is the standing practice for new privileged registrations. What is missing is the systemic guard: the registration record has no in-person attestation field, so a registration originally taken remotely for a non-privileged role can be promoted to a privileged role without a new in-person session, and the completed privileged accounts cannot be shown to have been proofed in person from the record alone. The attestation field and the promotion block are the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 inherits the Aurora Defense Systems incident response policy and adds a system-level procedure set that names the WS-X90 escalation chain, the declarable incident classes and the containment actions available on each subsystem. Both documents are held as signed revisions in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), which is the only source from which a controlled copy may be drawn, and each approved revision is republished to the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) for technician use. What is missing is the review cadence under the expanded scope: the organisation-level policy was last approved before the control set grew to 546 controls, and the WS-X90 procedure set has not yet completed its first at-least-annually review against the new set, so the procedures do not yet name the insider-threat branch or the spillage roles introduced by IR-4(6) and IR-9. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Incident response training is delivered by role. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) holds each individual's training record and acts as the gate on responder account issue: no responder account is created on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) without a completion date inside the annual window, and the 30-working-day clock starts from the provisioning record's role-assignment date. Scenario and checklist material is staged to the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) for delivery at operating locations. The core responder cadre is trained and current; what is missing is coverage of the ground support technicians who acquired WS-X90 access during the scope expansion, several of whom are past the 30-working-day bound, and continuous enforcement of the annual refresh — today currency is checked at recertification rather than at each session, so an account can outlive its training record by up to one recertification cycle. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned design injects scripted WS-X90 scenarios — navigation spoofing seen from the Timing Receiver and Navigation Sensor Interface, and maintenance-session abuse seen from the Maintenance Access Gateway — into the annual training cycle. Recorded and sanitised event sets are staged from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and replayed to the responder on the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019), which times each decision and scores the run against the expected containment sequence. The scenario library and the scoring rubric are drafted and reviewed; no scenario has yet been run against a responder, and the replay tooling is scheduled against the expanded-scope remediation plan. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Not implemented. WS-X90 has no automated incident response training environment; training is delivered from written scenario material rather than from a replay environment. A standalone replay capability hosted on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) with no route to any operational interface has been scoped but is unfunded, and the program has accepted delivering IR-2 and IR-2(1) without it for the current cycle. No claim of partial coverage is made. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The annual WS-X90 incident response test injects a controlled detection case into the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) and a controlled privileged-account-abuse case into the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), and records elapsed time from event generation to responder acknowledgement and to first containment action. The 2026 test ran both cases and the report is signed. What is missing is coordination with the recovery rehearsal: the controlled-recovery path on the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) was not exercised inside the incident window, so the joint case covering an incident that also requires a controlled restart has not been demonstrated. Because WS-X90 availability is categorised moderate, the joint case is scoped to an orderly bounded restart rather than to failover. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The plan is to schedule the annual incident response test and the contingency and recovery rehearsal into one window so that a declared incident drives the controlled-recovery path on the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) restart sequence is walked through jointly by the responder and the recovery operator. The joint scenario is written and the two plan owners have agreed the scope; the combined window is booked for the next annual cycle and has not yet run. WS-X90 availability is moderate, so the rehearsal objective is a bounded, orderly restart with a stated duration rather than continuity of service. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of IR-4 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Incident handling on WS-X90 is machine-driven from detection to containment. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) evaluates the platform security event stream against the WS-X90 detection rule set and opens an incident record in the protected incident store on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) within five minutes, carrying the rule identifier, the originating LRU and a reference to the raw event. Containment is then dispatched to the enforcement points: the Mission Computer (LRU-001) suspends the named non-essential mission service and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) drops the named external session, each inside thirty seconds and each written back to the record as a separate timestamped entry. No step in that chain requires an operator to transcribe an identifier. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Two WS-X90 incident classes bear directly on mission continuation, and the planned response is a defined safe state rather than continued full capability. On payload command-path compromise the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) stops accepting payload commands and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) latches to inhibit; on navigation integrity loss the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) reverts to its last validated navigation solution and raises a degraded-integrity flag. The class definitions and the latch semantics are agreed and captured in the interface control documents; the firmware changes on LRU-010 and LRU-011 are scheduled into the next load and no build carries them yet. Given moderate availability, the design deliberately accepts a reduced but safe capability rather than attempting to sustain full mission function through the incident. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) builds one incident timeline per incident from every reporting subsystem, keyed to platform time rather than to each source's local clock, so that mission compute, navigation, communications, payload, platform management and ground support events are read in a single ordering. Payload health and status records forwarded by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) join that timeline directly rather than being reconciled by hand afterwards. Where a contributing source has been silent for more than fifteen minutes the timeline carries an explicit silence marker, so an analyst distinguishes an absence of events from an absence of reporting. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned insider-threat branch of the WS-X90 incident handling procedure is entered on privileged-session anomalies observed at the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) — out-of-window sessions, credential use from an unassigned endpoint — and on out-of-policy account changes made on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013). A case in that branch is routed to a restricted responder list and is not visible to the standard on-call rotation. The trigger conditions are defined and the restricted list has a named approver; the case-visibility partition in the incident tooling is not yet built, so today such a case would be worked in the ordinary queue. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Coordination for WS-X90 insider-threat cases is planned around a fixed roster that includes, at a minimum, the Senior Agency Official for Privacy or designee and key cybersecurity personnel. The roster is to be bound to the restricted case record so that retrieval of Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) session captures and Security Log Collector (LRU-018) extracts is authorised by roster membership rather than by ordinary responder role. The roster composition is agreed with the privacy and security functions; the access binding in the incident tooling is not implemented, so retrieval is currently controlled by ordinary role membership. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

For at a minimum a known or suspected compromise or unauthorized access, the Product Security Engineer will release a sanitised WS-X90 incident summary to the appropriate Federal Cyber Center or other designated central department point of contact. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) assembles the summary from the incident record and strips mission payload and navigation content; the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) is the sole egress for that package and applies release review before transmission. The sanitisation profile and the release-review step are specified; the external reporting channel registration is outstanding, so no summary has yet been shared through it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Where an incident implicates a supplied component or a delivered software load, the planned handling identifies the affected release from the signed release metadata in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), notifies the supplying organisation, and places a staging hold on the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) so the implicated release cannot be pushed to a platform while the supplier response is outstanding. The metadata needed to make the identification is already present in LRU-020; the staging-hold flag on LRU-016 and its release-by-decision path are designed but not built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A named integrated incident response team is planned, drawn from program security engineering, platform engineering and ground support, able to deploy to a WS-X90 operating location within 72 hours. The deployment kit is a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) built from the current approved image held on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and provisioned with credentials scoped to the declared incident class and expiring on return. The roster and the call-out procedure are drafted; the deployment kit build has not been rehearsed and the scoped-credential profile does not yet exist on LRU-017. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

After containment the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) retains a read-only forensic capture of the affected Mission Computer (LRU-001) executable region and loaded module list, together with the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) platform integrity state word recorded at the time of the incident, and each capture is hashed at collection so a later analyst can prove the artifact was not altered in storage. What is missing is the analysis side: the program has no offline malicious-code analysis environment approved for WS-X90 artifacts, so captures are retained and hashed but are examined only by inspection of the module list rather than by execution or disassembly. Retention today is set at 90 days against a required 180. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Anomalous behaviour in the navigation and timing environment is captured at source. The Timing Receiver (LRU-005) emits an anomaly record when holdover is entered without a commanded cause, and the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) emits one when cross-sensor divergence exceeds the configured navigation integrity threshold. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) retains those records as a behaviour-analysis stream held separately from routine navigation telemetry, so a pattern can be examined without sampling the full telemetry volume. What is missing is analysis over time: the stream is retained and queryable but no baseline of normal divergence has been established, so an analyst can retrieve anomalies but cannot yet say whether a rate is abnormal. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Not implemented. There is no staffed security operations centre watching the WS-X90 exported event feed from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) outside program working hours, and no delegated authority to declare a WS-X90 incident sits outside the program engineering chain. Events raised overnight are queued and reviewed at the start of the next working day. Standing up a watch, or contracting one, is a program decision that has not been taken and no partial coverage is claimed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of IR-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Automated Tracking, Data Collection, and Analysis
n: Incident tracking is a machine function on WS-X90. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) mints one tracking identifier per incident at the moment the record opens and carries it through open, contained, eradicated and closed with no manual re-keying at any transition. Every transition is written to the protected incident store on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) with the acting identity and the transition timestamp, and the store rejects a transition whose timestamp precedes its predecessor, so the state history cannot be rewritten to look tidier than it was. Collection and analysis queries run against that store rather than against exported copies. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of IR-6 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Reporting is generated rather than typed. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) renders the initial WS-X90 incident report straight from the incident record — reportable-incident category, affected LRU list, detection time, containment time — and presents it for release review inside fifteen minutes of declaration, leaving unpopulated fields explicitly absent rather than blank-filled. Once released, the report leaves the platform through the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) on the approved reporting path; where that path is unavailable the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) carries an abbreviated form under the same release approval. Both paths write a delivery acknowledgement back against the tracking identifier, so an unacknowledged report is visible as such. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Where an incident is traced to an exploitable weakness in a fielded configuration, the incident record on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) names the affected baseline item held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) so the weakness is anchored to a specific configuration revision rather than described in prose. The report then goes to the WS-X90 system security engineering lead and to the responsible design authority. What is missing is the timing discipline and the second recipient: the routing to the design authority is manual and two of the four cases worked since the scope expansion reached it later than five working days after containment. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned supplier notice draws the affected part number and release identifier from the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) rather than from free text, and carries no mission data, no navigation data and no operating location. The template and the content-exclusion rules are drafted and have been reviewed by the program security function; the supplier distribution list and the transmission route are not yet established, so no notice has been issued under this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A named WS-X90 incident response support contact is reachable during program working hours and advises operators and technicians on reporting and on the bounded containment actions a technician may take from the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) without escalation. The current contact details are carried in the approved ground support procedure staged on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017). What is missing is cover outside program hours and a defined deputy: when the primary contact is unavailable the route falls back to the general engineering queue, which has no defined response expectation, and this is the same gap that IR-4(14) records at the watch level. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Automation Support for Availability of Information and Support
n: The current incident reporting procedure, contact roster and containment checklist are packaged as a signed bundle and held offline on the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019), refreshed from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) so a responder at a remote location does not need a network path to obtain them. The bundle signature verifies against the LRU-017 signing key before the laptop will render it. What is missing is refresh on roster change: the bundle is rebuilt on the quarterly image cycle rather than when the roster changes, so a deployed laptop can carry contact details up to three months stale. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The plan establishes a named working relationship with the external providers of the protected transport and network protection services behind the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007), with WS-X90 responders identified to those providers by role and by name and an agreed first action for a cross-boundary event. Contact records are drafted on the program side; the provider side has not been formally engaged and no joint exercise has been held, so a cross-boundary event today would begin with an introduction. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 incident response plan describes the responder structure, the declarable incident classes, the reportable-incident definitions, the metrics the program tracks and the resources committed to the capability. It is held as a signed release in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with a protected working copy on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) so that the plan is still readable during an incident that affects program information technology, and both copies are protected from unauthorised change. What is missing is the approval and distribution cycle under the expanded scope: the current revision predates the move to the 546-control set, has not been re-approved by the CISO/SAISO or equivalent, and its distribution list does not yet cover the ground support personnel who took on response roles with the expansion. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Spillage response on WS-X90 is split between containment and eradication. On declaration the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) blocks external sessions for the affected enclave and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) isolates the contaminated LRU port, both inside ten minutes, and the responder alert is issued on a path that does not traverse the contaminated segment. Eradication overwrites the affected regions of the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) with the approved sanitisation routine and produces a record naming every region cleared, and the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) is queried for every baseline that carried a copy of the affected artifact so that subsequently contaminated components are identified rather than assumed absent. What is missing is the assignment step and the alerting path: responsibility for spillage response is named in the procedure by role but not by individual, and the out-of-band alert route has been walked through on paper rather than exercised. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Spillage response training is planned on a cycle consistent with IR-2 for every individual authorised to handle WS-X90 mission data, covering the declaration route, the prohibition on discussing a spill over the contaminated path and the individual's own containment obligations. Completion will be recorded against the individual's provisioning record on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) alongside the incident response training record. The material is drafted; delivery is scheduled with the next IR-2 cycle and no completions have been recorded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Not implemented. WS-X90 has no documented degraded-operations procedure for continuing assigned tasks while contaminated storage is under corrective action. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) does support partitioned execution and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) can enforce a partition boundary, so the mechanism exists, but no procedure defines which tasks may continue, for how long, or at what point operations stop. Because WS-X90 availability is categorised moderate, the program has not treated continuation through a spill as a priority and has accepted a stop-and-remediate posture for now. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Not implemented. There is no defined handling for an individual exposed to WS-X90 information outside their access authorisation. Suspension of that individual's sessions on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014), quarantine and imaging of the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) used in the exposure, and a signed exposure acknowledgement as a precondition of access restoration are all specified in the draft spillage procedure but none is in force, and the draft has not been approved. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 maintenance policy and its implementing procedures are held as signed, version-controlled records in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with a named approving official and an at-least-annual review, the CNSSI 1253 parameter for this control. The policy was re-approved inside the current cycle. What is missing is the procedure set: it still describes the local maintenance path only and has not been updated for the nonlocal maintenance path implemented on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) in build 4.2, so technicians work that path from an engineering work instruction rather than an approved procedure. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of MA-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Maintenance, repair and replacement actions are scheduled, dispatched and closed out through the automated workflow on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), and the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) refuses any maintenance action that does not carry an open work order, so the workflow is a gate rather than a record. Closed-out actions are written to the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with the acting technician and the parts fitted. What is missing is coverage of the payload LRUs: maintenance records for the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) are still entered by hand after the fact and are not subject to the 30-day stale-record flag, so the record set is accurate for the platform management subsystem and incomplete for the payload interface subsystem. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of MA-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Before a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is issued, the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) compares its tool image against the approved tool baseline and blocks issue on any difference in file set, version or signature, recording the comparison against the laptop serial number. What is missing is the return leg: a laptop coming back from the field is re-shelved without re-inspection, so an unauthorized modification made during field use is only caught at the next issue rather than at return, and the record does not distinguish the two. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Diagnostic and test media are scanned on the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) with a signature set no more than seven days old before the media reaches any WS-X90 interface, and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) records the scan result and the signature-set date against the media serial number. Media presented at a platform interface without a current recorded scan is refused, so the scan is enforced at the point of use rather than only at the point of issue. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design requires maintenance equipment that has held WS-X90 information — principally the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) — to be verified clear, sanitized, destroyed or covered by a recorded exemption from a named authorizing official before it leaves the facility, with the release record joined to the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) session history that shows what the equipment was used for. The disposition procedure is drafted; there is no release record store, no join to session history, and no check today that prevents equipment leaving with no disposition recorded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Maintenance tool use is restricted at both ends. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) accepts a tool invocation only from an authenticated technician present on the current authorized-maintainer list, and revocation takes effect within one session. The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) will not launch a platform maintenance tool without a valid session token issued by LRU-014, so a laptop separated from the gateway is not a usable tool platform. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every maintenance tool invocation that runs with elevated platform privilege produces an audit record from the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) naming the tool, the technician identity and the privilege level, so privileged tool use is fully visible after the fact. Detection caught up with that visibility on 2026-11-14, when the rule raising an alert for a privileged invocation that falls outside an open work order was built on LRU-018; out-of-order privileged use now surfaces on its own rather than waiting for someone to go looking for it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 maintenance tools are baselined at first issue and are not inspected against a current approved patch level. The Configuration Repository (LRU-020) holds no per-tool approved patch level, and the issue workflow for the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) has no patch-level check or withhold action, so a tool can be issued with software older than the approved level without that being visible. The gap is carried on the plan of action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of MA-4 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) are logged with the event set defined in the WS-X90 audit policy for AU-1 — the CNSSI 1253 parameter points at that policy rather than a local list — covering session start, authentication outcome, every privileged command, every file transfer and session end. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) places each closed session in the review queue within one working day, so anomalous behaviour is reviewed against a defined queue rather than on request.
