This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The control is met on two paths. For in-place service, a session may be opened only from a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) whose baseline provides authentication, session encryption, endpoint integrity checking and audit forwarding at the platform level, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) requires a baseline attestation before establishing the session. For off-platform service, the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) clears mission information from the removed LRU while the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) retains its recovery material, and LRU-016 re-verifies the component image against the approved baseline before reconnection. Two gaps remain: contractor-supplied endpoints are still accepted on a manual waiver rather than an attestation, and the clear-and-verify path is automated only for Platform Management Subsystem LRUs — payload and navigation LRUs are removed under a manual procedure. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Authentication and Separation of Maintenance Sessions
n: Nonlocal maintenance sessions are authenticated on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) with a replay-resistant authenticator, so a captured exchange replayed against the gateway is refused. The session is carried on a dedicated VLAN on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) and a dedicated policy on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007), logically separated from mission traffic; maintenance frames observed on the switch carry the maintenance VLAN tag only. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Nonlocal maintenance traffic between the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) is protected for integrity and confidentiality with the approved algorithms listed in CNSSP 15 Annex B, the CNSSI 1253 parameter for this enhancement. Session keys are issued and held by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and appear in the platform key inventory by identifier. Negotiation is constrained to the approved set: a client offering only algorithms outside it is refused rather than downgraded, so the session fails closed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

At session close the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) destroys the session context and records a confirmed-terminated state, and a session context queried after close returns not found. What is missing is the network half: LRU-014 learns the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) connection state from a periodic poll rather than an explicit teardown acknowledgement, so a connection left established on LRU-007 can be reported as terminated for up to 60 seconds before the next poll corrects it, and the alert for an unconfirmed teardown fires on that delayed evidence. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of MA-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design covers maintenance by personnel without the required clearance or access approval: a cleared, technically qualified escort supervises the work, the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) is placed in a restricted maintenance mode that withholds mission-data and configuration functions, the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is booted from an uncleared-session image, and volatile mission information on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) is cleared before work starts. The restricted maintenance mode and the uncleared-session image are specified but not built, the escort procedure is drafted and not approved, and no alternate control has been written for a component that can be neither cleared in place nor physically detached. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 is categorized moderate for availability, so the maintenance response target is set proportionately: support or a serviceable spare for a failed Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) or Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) within 30 days of the failure being reported, with elapsed time recorded per failure. No continuous-availability or hot-spare commitment is made or implied. The support agreement covering the 30-day period is in negotiation and the failure register that would record report and arrival dates is not yet in service. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The preventive maintenance schedule sets a 12-month interval for the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) — retention-battery and recovery-media checks — the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) — oscillator ageing and holdover calibration — and the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) — connector and calibration checks — each recorded against the LRU serial number. The schedule is drafted but not approved, no serial-number due dates have been loaded, and no preventive check has yet been performed under it; maintenance on all three LRUs is currently corrective only. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Media protection direction for SYS-WSX90 is held as data, not as a shelf document: the policy and its five subordinate procedures - media access, marking, storage, transport and sanitization - sit in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) as signed, version-tagged artifacts, each with a named approver and a recorded review date, and LRU-020 raises a review-overdue flag once a date passes 12 months, which is the at-least-annual interval CNSSI 1253 sets for MP-1. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is the only endpoint that can publish a revision, so each effective revision carries an operator identity, a diff against its predecessor and the list of custodians and maintenance role holders it was distributed to. What is missing: the transport and sanitization-verification procedures are still drafts and carry no approver signature, so two of the five artifacts fail the signature check; and the media protection official is named in the policy header but the delegation has not been countersigned, leaving MP-1b evidenced by the policy text alone. Both gaps are carried as open media-protection remediation actions. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Access to WS-X90 media is a check-out decision, not a cabinet key. The scope CNSSI 1253 sets for MP-2 - all digital and non-digital media carrying information not cleared for public release - resolves on this program to the removable audit and recovery cartridges written by the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015), the provisioning volumes cut for field load, and the printed configuration and key-handling worksheets held with them. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) holds the media library register and gates every check-out on an identity present in the current custodian list, recording custodian, item serial and stated purpose; a request from any other identity is refused, no serial is released, and the refusal reaches the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) inside 60 seconds, where it is retained with the rest of the ground-support security record. LRU-015 writes a cartridge only against an open check-out, so a cartridge outside the library always resolves to a named holder. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Marking is currently manual and is being moved into the release path. The design puts label generation inside the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) write flow: when a removable volume is cut, LRU-017 will print a human-readable label carrying the distribution limitation, the handling caveat and the release record identifier issued by the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), and will refuse to close the release record until the label print is confirmed, so an unmarked volume cannot be signed out as released. Exemptions will be narrow by construction - only media that never leaves the named controlled provisioning area - and each exemption will be recorded against that area in LRU-020 rather than left to custodian judgement. Today custodians apply pre-printed caveat labels by hand against a paper log, which satisfies the intent of MP-3a inconsistently and gives no queryable exemption record; the label printer integration and the LRU-020 release-record field are scheduled work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Removable cartridges written by the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) carry audit and recovery material and are the only WS-X90 media that regularly sits outside a running LRU. When not in use they are held in the key-controlled media library inside the controlled maintenance area, and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) opens an inventory entry the moment a cartridge is removed from LRU-015 - serial, storage location, removal date - which stays open until a completed sanitization or destruction record closes it, which is how MP-4b protection-until-sanitized is carried on this program. What is missing: the monthly physical reconciliation is still a manual count transcribed into a spreadsheet rather than a count taken against the LRU-017 inventory, so a discrepancy is found late; the off-site spares cabinet at the support facility is not yet inside the same count; and nothing feeds cartridge inventory state to the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), so there is no platform-side view of outstanding media. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Nothing leaves the controlled maintenance area in the clear. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) will not release a volume for transport unless the volume is encrypted under a key issued by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), and will not complete the release until a transport record - authorized custodian, destination, seal number, release time - is bound to the volume serial; release is offered only to identities on the transport-authorized list, and the release event is exported to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which is where transport activity is reconstructed for an assessor. That covers MP-5a protection, MP-5d restriction to authorized personnel, and the outbound half of MP-5b and MP-5c. What is missing is the inbound half: courier hand-off and delivery receipts are still paper forms filed at the support facility and are not reconciled back into the transport record, so an open transport has no automated overdue or non-arrival alert and accountability during transit rests on the courier's signature alone. The receipt reconciliation feed is an open remediation action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of MP-6 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Review, Approve, Track, Document, and Verify
n: MP-6 sanitization itself is fielded and evidenced on this program; the review, approval, tracking and verification wrapper that MP-6(1) adds is designed and not yet built. The design hosts a sanitization record on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) carrying the approving reviewer, the media serial and category, the method applied, the operator who performed it, the verification result and the disposal action, and refuses completion while the approver and operator are the same identity or while the verification result is empty - a two-person rule enforced by the record rather than by the custodian. Completed records are to be exported to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) and referenced from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) inventory entry so a cartridge cannot be retired without one. Today the same sequence runs on a paper sanitization form with a wet signature, which is auditable only by pulling the binder and gives no automatic check that verification actually happened before disposal. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Sanitization tooling on WS-X90 is software: the wipe utility fielded on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) for library cartridges and the reduced field utility on the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019). The planned test is a coupon: write a known marker pattern to a sample cartridge of each media type in service, sanitize it with the fielded utility and the published procedure, then read the device back through a raw path and confirm no instance of the pattern is recoverable, recording tool version, operator and result. The interval is the at-least-annual frequency CNSSI 1253 sets for MP-6(2), with a re-test inside 30 days of any utility version change, and a failing coupon suspends that version for WS-X90 media. The procedure is drafted and the coupon media has been identified; no coupon test has been executed yet, so no assurance is claimed that the intended sanitization is achieved. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No intake sanitization capability is fielded. Portable storage devices arriving from a vendor or returning with a gap in their chain of custody are handled today only by the MP-7 registry restriction - an unregistered or unowned serial will not mount - and by malware scanning on receipt, neither of which is the nondestructive wipe before first connection that MP-6(3) calls for. The intake station on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the corresponding mount block on the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) are scoped but unfunded, and no partial credit is claimed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Media use on WS-X90 is restricted in two independent places. On the platform, the Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) refuse mass-storage class enumeration on their maintenance ports unless the device serial is in the signed removable-device allow-list distributed from the Configuration Repository (LRU-020); the port stays electrically enabled for diagnostic use but the storage function is never bound, and a refusal record naming the serial and port is emitted within 60 seconds. LRU-001 additionally holds write access to an allow-listed device disabled in flight configuration, so removable media is a read path only. On the ground, the approved portable-storage registry in LRU-020 binds every serial to a named custodian, an issue date and a category, and marks an entry vacant when the custodian record lapses; the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) mount nothing whose serial is absent or vacant, which is how the no-identifiable-owner prohibition in MP-7b is enforced rather than asserted. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Physical and environmental protection for WS-X90 is carried at the facility level by Aurora Defense Systems and inherited by the system, so PE-1 is being written as a programme-specific procedure set rather than adopted wholesale from the corporate estate policy. The drafted set names the Platform Lead as accountable official, scopes the integration bay around the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) and the provisioning area around the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), and fixes an annual reissue cadence plus an event trigger on any facility move. Nothing has been issued yet; the draft is with programme security for first review and the annual review clock starts at first issue. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A facility access roster is maintained for the three WS-X90 controlled spaces: the provisioning area holding the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), the maintenance bay holding the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014), and the controlled storage from which the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is drawn. Badge credentials are issued against roster entries and the roster is reviewed annually by the Platform Lead. What is missing is the removal side: roster strike-off and badge revocation are done manually on notification from the personnel function, and two sampled leavers were removed 9 and 12 working days after departure against the 5-working-day target. A POA&M action to drive removals from the personnel system feed rather than from manual notification is open. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of PE-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The protected equipment bay holding the Mission Computer (LRU-001), the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) is behind a second reader with its own access list, so a credential that opens the outer facility door does not open the bay. The bay list is a strict subset of the facility roster and refusals are logged at the reader. What is not yet in place is the reconciliation: the bay list is maintained by hand against the facility roster rather than derived from it, so a facility-roster removal does not automatically remove bay access, and the reader event log is not yet exported to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) for correlation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Transmission media are protected in two distinct ways because they are two distinct problems. Copper mission-data runs between the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) are carried in locked conduit and sealed tray inside the facility. RF and sensor runs — the antenna feed at the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) and the harness entering the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) — are protected by sealed, witness-marked connectors instead, because conduit is not available on the flight-side runs. Both are partial: two conduit access covers on the LRU-007 to LRU-009 route are currently secured with a padlock rather than a serialised seal, and the connector seal serials for the LRU-006 harness are recorded on the bench sheet but not yet posted to the airframe record. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Output control on WS-X90 is achieved by removing the output paths rather than by controlling access to them. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) ship in a hardened build with print spooling, removable-media write and external display output disabled at the driver policy level; device attachment attempts are refused and written to the endpoint log. Screen placement in the provisioning area was surveyed and both positions face away from the corridor glazing. No printer exists in either controlled space. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of PE-6 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The facility already runs intrusion alarms and cameras over the WS-X90 spaces, but they are a facility service with no interface to the system. The planned build adds a one-way export of forced-door and after-hours motion events into the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) across a data diode, so that a physical event can be correlated against chassis-intrusion telemetry from the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013). The one-way direction is the design constraint: nothing from the alarm estate may reach a WS-X90 component. Diode procurement is on the sustainment order and the LRU-018 ingest schema for physical events is drafted but not built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Monitoring today stops at the outer facility door, which cannot tell whether the person who opened a maintenance session on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) was in the bay at the time. The planned design gives the maintenance bay its own reader and forwards bay-scoped badge events to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) carrying a bay identifier, so LRU-018 can raise a session-without-presence anomaly. The reader and cabling are specified; the LRU-018 correlation rule is designed but the bay reader has not been installed and no bay-scoped events exist yet. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Visitor records for the provisioning area around the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) are kept for a full year and reviewed by the Platform Lead on a quarterly cycle, with anomalies reported to the System Security Engineer. Retention and reporting are working. The gap is review cadence discipline and export: the last four review intervals were 88, 90, 97 and 84 days, so the 90-day ceiling was breached once, and the records are still reviewed in the badge system rather than mirrored to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which means a visitor anomaly cannot be correlated with system events. Both items are carried in the remediation plan. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Visitor sign-in for the WS-X90 areas is currently a paper book kept at the provisioning area desk, which is why review is manual and anomaly detection is retrospective. The planned change moves sign-in onto the site badge system, adds a nightly export into the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), and drives an automatic review prompt to the Platform Lead once 90 days have elapsed since the last recorded review. The badge system already supports visitor enrolment; the work is the export job and the prompt rule, neither of which is built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Not implemented. Visitor records are held in the site badge system in its default schema, which carries personal fields beyond what WS-X90 needs, and no minimised export view has been defined. This is a privacy-driven enhancement on a system whose privacy analysis has not yet been run, so no programme work has started. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Power feeds to the mission rack run in protected raceway from a lockable distribution panel, with the breakers serving the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) labelled to the LRU identifier. The panel schedule was cleaned up during the last integration stand-down. Two gaps remain: the LRU-011 feed still shares a breaker with the bench lighting circuit for the payload interface bench, which is a non-programme load, and the panel lock is a common-key type rather than a programme-controlled key. Availability here is treated proportionately — the categorisation for WS-X90 is moderate, so this is about protecting the feeds from damage and mis-operation, not about redundant supply. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The payload interface bench carries a guarded emergency cutoff within arm's reach of the operator position that drops the supply to the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) while leaving the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) monitoring rail up, so the state at the moment of the cut can be read back afterwards. Measured drop time across ten activations was between 0.6 and 1.1 seconds. The cutoff is mushroom-head with a strike shroud and is keyed to reset, so it cannot be re-armed by a passer-by. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 is categorised moderate for availability, so the emergency power design targets an orderly shutdown rather than transition to long-term alternate power, and the narrative deliberately claims nothing more. The planned uninterruptible supply covers the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) for 15 minutes of ride-through, long enough to flush the LRU-015 audit buffer and bring the rack down cleanly. Load calculations are done and the unit is specified; procurement is against the next sustainment order and no shutdown script yet exists that sequences the buffer flush. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Not implemented at programme level. Emergency lighting on the egress route from the provisioning area is a facility service that WS-X90 inherits, and the programme has neither surveyed the route against the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) position nor obtained a coverage or test record from the facility. No programme action has started. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Fire detection and suppression over the integration bay and the provisioning area is a facility system, and the programme's planned work is to establish that it holds up on an energy source independent of the building supply while the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) and Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) racks are installed and powered. That means obtaining the independent-source service record, adding both spaces by name to the annual facility check scope, and witnessing the check once. None of the three has been done; the request to the facility is raised. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Detection Systems — Automatic Activation and Notification
n: Detection in the WS-X90 spaces activates automatically today and notifies the site fire response desk, but it does not notify the Platform Lead in the same alarm cycle and it emits nothing that WS-X90 can consume. The planned change adds the Platform Lead to the notification group and emits a dated event to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) so the alarm can be reconciled against Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) shutdown telemetry — which matters because a thermal event and an unexplained shutdown currently appear as two unrelated records. Both changes ride on the same facility interface work as PE-6(1). This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Suppression Systems — Automatic Activation and Notification
n: Not implemented. The provisioning area holding the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is unstaffed overnight and at weekends, and the programme has not confirmed whether suppression in that space runs in automatic mode during those periods or is switched to manual by the facility out of hours. No mode log has been requested and no test activation has been witnessed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Environmental monitoring is genuinely continuous on the system side and only periodic on the facility side. The Timing Receiver (LRU-005) reports oven temperature and the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) reports bay temperature to the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) once per second, and LRU-013 alarms on an out-of-band reading within seconds — which is why the timing holdover budget is defensible at all. Humidity, by contrast, is read from a facility gauge on the twice-daily walk-round, so a humidity excursion between walk-rounds is invisible. Fitting a humidity sensor onto the LRU-013 telemetry loop is the open corrective action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Not implemented. There are wet services in the ceiling void above the integration bay holding the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), but the isolation valves have not been identified on the bay drawing, their reachability has not been checked, and duty staff have not been briefed on their location. No programme action has started. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Movement of line-replaceable units across the facility boundary is authorised on a movement docket naming serial number and receiving custodian, and the movement is posted against the asset entry in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). The spares pool for the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is fully covered. The gap is timeliness and closure: postings are batched weekly rather than same-day, so LRU-020 lags physical reality by up to five days, and three units in the last quarter show an outbound movement as their last posting while being physically present on site. A same-day posting rule and a reconciliation sweep are the open actions. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Alternate work site use is real for WS-X90 because the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is a conditional-status endpoint that travels to depot and field locations. The planned control set fixes an approved site list, requires locked storage between sessions, forbids unattended sessions, and permits no network connection other than the link to the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014). Draft rules exist and have been walked with two technicians, but the approved site list has not been signed off, no effectiveness assessment has been run at any site, and the incident reporting path from a field site is still the general corporate line rather than a programme contact. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of PE-18 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Hardware marking is done at two levels because the two populations are handled by different people. Mission-side protected units — the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) — carry an etched nameplate marking stating the highest impact level they may process, positioned for in-situ reading with covers fitted, and the marking is on the issue-C nameplate drawing so it is reproduced at every build. Ground support units — the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) — carry an equivalent label, and the LRU-019 label additionally states conditional-use status so it is not signed out of storage for an unrelated task. A marking survey of the controlled storage inventory found no unmarked endpoint. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The facility holding the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and the controlled storage for the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is an existing site, so PE-23 for WS-X90 is a hazard-consideration exercise rather than a siting decision. The planned work is to obtain the site flood, seismic and adjacent-industrial assessments, record which hazards cannot be engineered out, and carry those forward into the WS-X90 risk register instead of leaving them closed in the facility file. The assessments have been requested from the estates function; none have been received and no register entries exist. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has a system security plan but no system-level planning policy and procedure set governing how that plan and the architecture, concept of operations and rules of behaviour are produced and maintained. The planned build holds the set signed in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), reviews it at least annually per the CNSSI 1253 parameter for PL-1 and after any boundary or authorization state change, and names the designated planning official on every revision. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of PL-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Rules of behaviour exist for WS-X90, are acknowledged before account enablement on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014), the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) accounts, and are reviewed annually. The gap is in re-acknowledgement: LRU-014 checks that an acknowledgement exists but not that it is against the current revision, so a holder who acknowledged an earlier version keeps access after a revision, and there is no automatic disablement at the ten working day mark. LRU-017 enforces the current revision correctly and is the pattern the gateway will be brought to. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Social Media and External Site/Application Usage Restrictions
n: The current WS-X90 rules of behaviour say nothing about social media, external sites or the reuse of Aurora-issued identifiers off-platform. The planned revision adds clauses covering the posting of build identifiers, subsystem and LRU names, integration bay imagery and schedule information, and the use of Aurora identifiers or authentication secrets to create external accounts. The configuration half already holds: neither the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) nor the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) has a general-purpose browsing path, so the rule will be backed by the absence of the route. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has no security concept of operations; operating intent is spread across the security plan and the maintenance procedures. The planned document describes operation across mission phases, the decision authority at each phase, entry to and exit from maintenance and provisioning windows, and Mission Computer (LRU-001) behaviour on a security event. Consistent with the moderate availability objective it will state a controlled mission abort and recover posture rather than continuous failover, which is what the platform actually does, and will be reviewed at each baseline change board and at least annually. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A WS-X90 security architecture description exists in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and states which security functions each subsystem carries. Two things are incomplete. The description records carried and inherited functions for four of the six subsystems and does not yet record the assumptions made about external dependencies, so PL-8a is met in part. And while every function allocated to the Mission Computer (LRU-001) resolves to a named element in the approved build manifest, the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) flow-policy allocations do not, and they are currently shown as covered rather than carried as open gaps with an owner and a target baseline. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Defense in depth is real on both paths but the independence claim does not fully hold. Externally, the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) link-layer admission policy and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) flow policy are generated from separate configuration sources and neither derives its rules from the other. On the payload command path the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) segment policy, the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) command validation and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) arm authorization form three layers, and a rejection at any one stops the command, but LRU-009 and LRU-010 currently draw part of their segment definition from the same generated file, so a single error in that file can weaken two layers at once. Separating those sources is the open item. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Supplier diversity between the boundary and internal enforcement points is not achieved. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) both derive their enforcement from one vendor switching stack, so a single vendor defect or advisory reaches both layers at once and the depth described under PL-8(1) is shallower than it appears. No second-source assessment has been performed and no procurement action has been opened. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Malicious code protection is centrally managed for every WS-X90 LRU from the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016), with the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) holding the authoritative status view and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) the single alert path. Flaw remediation is centrally managed for the mission computing, navigation, communications and platform management LRUs but the payload subsystem LRUs are still scheduled by hand, which is the open gap. The spam protection element of the CNSSI 1253 parameter for PL-9 has no applicable service on WS-X90, which carries no messaging or mail transfer function, and is recorded as not applicable with that rationale rather than claimed as met. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 selects one control baseline, PROFILE-WSX90-TAILORED, held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). SP 800-53B High is recorded as the starting baseline, selected from the high water mark of the C high, I high, A moderate categorization, with the CNSSI 1253 allocation applied over it and three named overlays after that. Every control in the resulting set carries an ordered selection trail, so the baseline can be read as a derivation rather than as an asserted list. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Tailoring of the WS-X90 baseline is recorded as individual events in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), each naming the control, the action, the driver and the approving authority. Replaying the recorded events over SP 800-53B High reproduces the effective control set exactly, so the difference between the published baseline and what WS-X90 actually carries is reconstructible from the record without reference to anyone's memory. A control introduced into the set without a matching event fails the baseline review and the rejection is recorded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Aurora personnel security policy and the WS-X90 supporting procedures set the screening levels, national eligibility gating, access agreement terms and termination and transfer handling that the program applies. The approved revision is held as a signed release in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and disseminated to every role that provisions accounts from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), and a named official is designated to manage it. What is missing is currency: the last approved revision predates the national eligibility gating change made during the scope expansion, so the enforced behaviour on LRU-017 is stricter than the published procedure describes, and the at-least-annually review is overdue. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every WS-X90 position that can obtain a privileged account carries a recorded risk designation with the screening criteria that follow from it, and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) refuses to issue a privileged account for a position whose designation record is absent. What is missing is the review trigger set: designations are reviewed on the annual cycle, but the additional triggers — position description update and position vacancy — are not wired into the personnel process, so a description rewritten mid-year does not force a designation review until the next annual pass. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Screening is a hard precondition of WS-X90 account creation. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) holds each individual's completed screening record and the level it was completed at, and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) will not create an account until LRU-017 confirms a completed screening at the level the position risk designation requires. The record is re-verified at each account recertification cycle rather than checked once at issue, so an account whose holder's screening lapses is caught at the next cycle and refused renewal. Refusals are recorded with the reason. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 mission data and privileged maintenance sessions are restricted to individuals whose citizenship status is recorded and verified against the program's national eligibility requirement. The verification is held on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), is set by the program security function rather than by the requesting individual or the provisioning technician, and is enforced as a hard gate: the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) privileged maintenance roster is built only from individuals carrying a verified eligibility record, and an account request without one is refused rather than issued with an advisory flag. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Termination processing disables WS-X90 access on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) within the same day for an involuntary termination and within five working days for a voluntary one, updates the individual's provisioning record on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), places the issued credential on the revocation list held by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) so the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) rejects it at the next session attempt, and records recovery of any assigned Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) or issued token. What is missing is the exit interview content and the retention step: exit interviews are held but do not follow a defined security topic list, and there is no documented process for retaining program access to information formerly controlled by the terminated individual, which has left two orphaned data sets on the ground support share. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned exit process notifies departing individuals who held WS-X90 access of the legally binding post-employment obligations for protecting program information and takes a signed acknowledgement, filed against the individual's provisioning record on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) as a precondition of closing that record. The obligation text has been settled with the legal function; the exit interview script has not been updated to include it and no acknowledgement has yet been captured. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Termination is machine-driven. A termination action entered in the Aurora personnel feed disables the individual's mapped WS-X90 accounts on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) and raises a notification to the security operations distribution held by the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) inside sixty minutes, with no technician performing the disable by hand. A feed entry that maps to no WS-X90 account produces a recorded no-op rather than a silent drop, so a mapping error is visible as an unmatched entry rather than as an account that was never disabled. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

On reassignment or transfer, the WS-X90 access set is reviewed against the operational need of the new position and accesses no longer required on need-to-know grounds are removed or disabled on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), with the change confirmed against the individual's provisioning record on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017). What is missing is the ten-working-day discipline and the notification step: transfers are worked in the monthly provisioning batch, so three of the seven transfers since the scope expansion exceeded ten working days, and no automatic notification is raised to the receiving and losing managers. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 access agreement is signed before any account is issued and re-signed at least annually or whenever the agreement text is updated. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) holds the signed agreement date and treats it as a precondition of both account issue and each recertification, so an account cannot be renewed against a lapsed agreement. Publishing a new agreement revision automatically raises a re-sign requirement against every holder of the superseded revision rather than waiting for their next anniversary. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned change adds the legally binding post-employment obligations to the WS-X90 access agreement itself and takes the individual's acknowledgement at initial access rather than only at exit, recorded on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) beside the signed agreement. The clause is drafted and agreed with the legal function; it has not yet been published as an agreement revision, so no current holder has acknowledged it at grant. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

External providers whose personnel hold WS-X90 credentials or maintenance access carry contractual personnel security requirements, including a duty to notify the organizational security manager of any transfer or termination of those personnel as soon as possible and not to exceed one working day. Compliance is monitored by reconciling the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) session roster and the issued Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) inventory against each provider's personnel list. What is missing is coverage and cadence: two of the five current provider agreements predate the one-working-day clause and carry a five-day term instead, and the reconciliation has been run twice in the last six months rather than monthly. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A formal sanctions process for WS-X90 policy breaches is planned, triggered by defined conditions including bypassing the maintenance session controls on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and suppressing or deleting records on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), with notification to the program security manager and the individual's line manager within five working days of initiation, naming the individual and the reason. The organisation has a general disciplinary process; the WS-X90 trigger conditions and the notification path have been drafted but not adopted, so no program-specific initiation has occurred. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The planned update states the security responsibilities carried by each WS-X90 role that can provision accounts from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) or sign a configuration baseline into the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), and references the applicable position description revision from the individual's provisioning record so the responsibilities in force at the time of a grant can be reconstructed. Draft text exists for the two provisioning roles; the baseline-signing roles have not been drafted and no position description has been reissued. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 inherits the Aurora enterprise risk management policy but has no system-level risk assessment policy of its own, so the annual review parameter is currently met at the enterprise level only. The planned build places the system-level policy and its procedures in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) as a signed set, adds the designated risk-assessment official and dissemination list as record fields rather than prose, and wires the twelve-month staleness flag into the release promotion gate so a lapsed policy stops a build rather than being caught at audit. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 is categorized confidentiality high, integrity high, availability moderate. The record in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) carries a separate impact rationale per objective and a dated authorizing official approval, and it is the same record that selects SP 800-53B High as the starting baseline and drives the CNSSI 1253 allocation, so the categorization cannot drift away from the control set derived from it. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) stamps the three-value categorization into every artifact header it emits. A conflicting H-M-M figure in an older configuration example was rejected during the reference rebuild and the resolution is recorded with the profile derivation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of RA-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Supply chain risk for WS-X90 is currently assessed once at procurement and not refreshed. The planned build produces a standing assessment for each of the three externally procured LRUs, the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), covering counterfeit part risk, firmware provenance and named sub-tier suppliers for every programmable element, reissued at least annually and within thirty days of a supplier, foundry or waveform-vendor change. What is missing is the assessment itself, the supplier-change trigger and the link from the assessment into the criticality analysis; nothing is fielded yet. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No all-source intelligence channel supports the WS-X90 risk analysis. Threat input today is limited to open vendor advisories handled by the Product Security Engineer. Neither the intelligence-source field on the risk register in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) nor the path from an intelligence report to a Security Log Collector (LRU-018) detection rule exists, and no clearance arrangement for receiving such reporting on the program has been established. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has no representation of the current threat environment inside the platform; boundary policy is static between baselines. The planned design keeps a named threat state on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), refreshed on each ground-segment bulletin and at least weekly, and gives the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) a distinct flow policy per state, with every policy load written to the gateway audit stream. The state machine, the policy set and the bulletin ingest are all still to be built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of RA-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) pulls its vulnerability signature set from the approved feed mirrored in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), and the mirror is refreshed on a weekly schedule with a signed timestamp. What is missing is the enforcement: the workstation does not yet compare the signature timestamp against the 24-hour window the CNSSI 1253 parameter for RA-5(2) sets before a scan starts, so a scan can currently run on a stale set, and the signature identifier is written into the scan log but not into the scan report header a reviewer reads. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Discoverable information is handled as two separate exposures. On the network side the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) has been stripped of service banners and version strings and is surveyed quarterly from outside the boundary; one host-name leak on an error path remains open and is tracked for the next configuration change. On the RF side the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) protects mission traffic, but the acquisition preamble and idle keep-alive pattern have not been surveyed by an off-platform receiver, so no statement can yet be made about what a passive listener recovers from those states. Corrective action timing is defined for the network survey and not for the RF survey. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Credentialed scanning of the Mission Computer (LRU-001) baseline runs only from a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) session that the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) has authorized under a named privileged scan role. The role is issued per scan window, never held standing on the laptop, and is revoked as part of session teardown, so the scan credential is only meaningful while the gateway is holding the window open. Refusals are written to the gateway audit stream with the requesting session identity. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The three input streams a multi-hop view needs, vulnerability scan output, configuration drift reports and audit alerts, all reach the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) today but are read separately by an analyst. The planned build joins them per build identifier against the approved segmentation map and emits a multi-hop finding naming the ordered LRU sequence and the permitted flow that connects them. Neither the join nor the finding type exists yet, and the segmentation map is not currently machine-readable to LRU-018. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Aurora operates no public reporting channel for vulnerabilities in WS-X90 components. Reports arriving by other routes are handled case by case by the Product Security Engineer with no intake register, no receipt commitment and no recorded decision authority. Establishing the channel is an Aurora-level action that the program has not yet raised, and the intake register in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) has not been specified. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every finding from the completed assessment carries a response decision in the risk register in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), with an accepting authority named on each acceptance and a POA&M item on each mitigation, so the response practice itself is established. Two things are missing: the fifteen working day decision clock is tracked in a spreadsheet rather than enforced by the register, and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) still reports a baseline as compliant when an open finding against it has no decision, which removes the signal that should stop that baseline from shipping. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A criticality analysis exists for WS-X90 baseline 4.2 and classifies the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) integrity monitor, the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) arm and inhibit path and the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) root-of-trust verification as mission-critical with a named protection allocation for each. What is missing is coverage and cadence: functions in the ground support subsystem are unclassified, the supply chain measures column is populated for only two of the three mission-critical entries, and the analysis is refreshed at design reviews but not at every baseline change board. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has no threat hunting capability. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) evaluates fixed detection rules against the exported telemetry stream and retains alerts, but retains no searchable corpus behind them, so an analyst cannot run a hypothesis-driven search over past data. The continuous employment frequency the CNSSI 1253 parameter for RA-10 sets is therefore not met in any degree, and neither the workspace nor the retention needed to start is funded in the current baseline. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Aurora holds the WS-X90 system and services acquisition policy and its supporting procedures as a controlled document set in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020); the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is the only workstation authorised to publish a new revision, and each revision carries signed release metadata naming the designated acquisition security official and the roles the issue was disseminated to. What is missing is enforcement of the review cadence: the repository stores the review date but does not yet block an expired procedure from being cited in a procurement package, and the last full reissue predates the expansion of the tailored profile from 74 to 546 controls, so the procedure set does not yet describe the acquisition actions the new SA, SR and CM enhancements require. Remediation is tracked against the acquisition procedure refresh. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Aurora intends to carry WS-X90 security engineering as a discrete funded line rather than as overhead absorbed into subsystem budgets. The planned build is a resourcing record, maintained alongside the program work breakdown, that names the security effort allocated to each of the six subsystems and the ground support toolchain refresh covering the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019). Nothing is in place today beyond the draft: the line item has not been established in the programming submission and no subsystem allocation has been agreed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every WS-X90 build is admitted to the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) through an intake gate that requires a life-cycle phase tag — design, development, integration, qualification or sustainment — and the named security role accountable for that phase; the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) refuses to provision an LRU from a build that lacks either field. Risk decisions taken during a phase are attached to the same build record, which is what makes the risk process part of the life cycle rather than a parallel activity. The gap is coverage: the intake gate is enforced for mission computing, communications and platform management builds, but payload interface firmware is still delivered by the supplier as a sustainment drop without a phase tag, so those builds are admitted under a manual waiver. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 preproduction integration bench is today an engineering asset built by hand and protected informally. The planned change is to treat the bench as a controlled environment: provision it from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) using the same signed baseline that flight units receive, and physically bar the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) from bridging the bench to any operational network segment. Neither is in place — bench builds are still assembled from developer images, and the laptop is currently permitted on both sides. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Use of Live or Operational Data
n: Operational mission data is occasionally needed on the WS-X90 preproduction bench to reproduce a fielded defect. Aurora plans two controls around it: a recorded, expiring approval that names the data set and the approving authority, held with the provisioning record on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017); and a handling rule that raises the bench and the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) to the protection level of the flight Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) for as long as the approval is live, with sanitisation before the laptop returns to general support use. Today the approval is informal and the handling rule is unwritten. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 navigation and timing hardware is the part of the platform with the shortest supplier production horizon, and Aurora has no dated refresh plan for it. The planned build is a refresh schedule holding, for the Timing Receiver (LRU-005), Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006), a replacement decision point tied to the vendor end-of-production date recorded against each item. Availability for WS-X90 is categorised moderate, so the schedule targets planned replacement inside the sustainment cycle rather than hot spare inventory. Nothing is scheduled today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 LRU procurement packages carry the security functional and assurance requirements allocated to that LRU by control id drawn from the tailored profile, together with the acceptance criteria the first article must meet; the resulting acceptance record is filed against the LRU entry in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) inventory entry is not marked accepted until it exists. That path works for the LRUs procured after the tailoring baseline was set. It does not cover the three ground support items bought before it — their packages reference the superseded 74-control set, so the allocated requirements for the SA, SR and CM enhancements added by the re-derivation were never placed on contract and are being retrofitted through engineering change rather than acquisition. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The suppliers of the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) deliver a functional properties description for every security function exposed at the LRU boundary. Each description states the inputs the function accepts, the outputs and error states it can return, and the externally observable behaviour of every enforcement decision — including what an assessor sees when the function denies. The descriptions are held against the LRU record in the Configuration Repository and are what the assessment procedures for the boot and key-use controls are written from, so a change to an enforcement behaviour surfaces as a documentation delta before it surfaces as a test failure. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Design and Implementation Information for Controls
n: Security-relevant external interface specifications and high-level design are held for the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) at a depth that lets an assessor trace each enforcement decision back to a named interface rather than to a subsystem. LRU-003 and LRU-007 additionally have low-level design available for review under the supplier agreement. LRU-011 does not: the interlock supplier has delivered the interface specification and a block-level design, but the low-level design covering the authorization state machine is still being negotiated, which leaves the independent-authorization argument resting on the supplier's assertion rather than on reviewed design. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Aurora plans to require the mission software supplier to demonstrate the development life cycle actually used for the release that ships, rather than the process described in the proposal — the systems engineering method, the security engineering method, and the verification and quality gates — evidenced against the build record for the Mission Computer (LRU-001) software held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). The demonstration is planned as a walkthrough at each qualification gate. No walkthrough has been held and the contractual hook does not yet exist. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 LRUs are delivered with the approved hardened configuration already applied: the delivered configuration hash is compared with the approved baseline recorded in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) at first power-on and there is no post-delivery hardening step to forget. The Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) reapplies the same approved configuration as the default on reinstallation and recovery, so a recovered LRU comes up hardened rather than at vendor defaults. The gap is on the recovery side: the default-reapply path is verified for mission computing and platform management LRUs, but the payload interface LRUs recover to a supplier default profile that a technician must then correct by hand, which is exactly the manual step the control exists to remove. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The commercial information assurance products inside the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) were selected on functional grounds; their evaluation status was not a selection criterion and is not recorded anywhere the program can query. Aurora plans to record, per product, either the NIAP Protection Profile it was evaluated against or — where no profile applies to the technology type and the product enforces its policy with cryptography — the FIPS 140 validation or NSA approval by certificate number. The register does not exist yet and two of the three product certificate positions are unknown. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Functions, Ports, Protocols, and Services in Use
n: Each WS-X90 supplier declares the functions, ports, protocols and services its LRU uses in operational configuration, and that declaration is the set the platform permits: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) external rule set and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) segment policy are generated from the declarations rather than maintained by hand, and anything undeclared is denied by default. The Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) declaration is the tightest on the platform, listing a fixed set of sensor bus services with no management protocol exposed. A declaration change is a configuration change: the generated rule set is rebuilt and the delta is reviewed before the release ships. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has no PIV-based credential path. Technicians authenticate to the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) and Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) using the platform's own credential store, and no approved-products selection has been made for credential readers because no reader is fitted. Nothing is implemented against this control today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 ships two documentation sets that are treated as configuration items rather than deliverable prose. The administrator set covers the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and Platform Management Controller (LRU-013): secure configuration and operation of every privileged maintenance function, the effective use of each security mechanism the technician touches, and the known configuration weaknesses a technician must avoid — reissued with each configuration baseline change so a technician never works from a set that predates the baseline on the unit. The operator set covers the mission software on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the payload health displays fed by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012), and describes each security function an operator can invoke together with the behaviour the system exhibits when that function denies an action, which is the part operators most often lack. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 security architecture description names, per subsystem, the engineering principles applied and the specific design decision that carries each one — so a reviewer can follow a principle to a mechanism instead of to a statement of intent. The mission computing sections are written to that depth: least privilege resolves to the service manifest check on the Platform Management Controller, hierarchical trust resolves to the boot measurement chain, and mediated access resolves to a named enforcement point. The Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) sections are equally complete. What is missing is the same treatment for the navigation and timing subsystem and for the payload interface: the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) sections still assert principles without naming the design decision that carries them, which is the failure mode the control exists to prevent. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Mission applications on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) reach payload command authority today through a thin wrapper over the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) register map, which means the abstraction leaks: an application that knows the register layout can compose a command the wrapper never intended. The planned change presents payload command authority as a single named abstraction with one entry point and no register-level alternative, so that the mediation the interface controller performs cannot be bypassed by an application that understands the hardware. The abstraction is specified but not yet built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Mission applications at different trust levels on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) currently share one message-passing mechanism and one switch queue, so a fault or a flood in a low-trust application is felt by a high-trust one. The planned separation gives each trust level its own queue with its own quota on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) VLAN, removing the shared mechanism that would otherwise be a common path between them. The queue split is designed; the switch quota configuration has not been written. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Mission Computer (LRU-001) is built in declared layers with the security enforcement services below the mission applications and no upward calls, and that layering is documented and reviewed. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004) is the incomplete half: navigation integrity checking is being separated into its own loadable module with a declared interface so a sensor fusion change cannot alter the integrity check without a separate signed module release, but the current build still compiles fusion and integrity checking into one image, so the separation exists on paper and not in the delivered firmware. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 initialisation is currently ordered by convention rather than by a declared dependency graph, and one circularity is known: a platform service consumed by the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) itself waits on navigation data during a cold start. The planned change makes initialisation a directed acyclic graph with the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) completing before any service it protects, and removes the navigation circularity by giving the sensor interface a boot-time default that does not require navigation. The graph is drawn; the boot sequence has not been changed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Payload command mediation should happen once, at the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010), and it should be cheap enough that no mission application on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) has an incentive to look for a faster path around it. The planned design fixes a mediation budget of 5 ms on the command path so that mediation is not the reason a developer proposes a bypass. The budget is set in the interface specification; the mediation path has not been measured against it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) and Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) both use pooled buffers, and a buffer released by one security domain can today be handed to another without being cleared. The planned change removes the sharing: buffers are partitioned per domain, and any buffer that does cross a domain boundary is zeroised before reuse. The partitioning is specified for both LRUs and neither has shipped it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) authorization path is the smallest security-critical body of code on WS-X90 and the program intends to keep it small enough to review in full: a bounded state machine, no dynamic memory allocation, and no more externally reachable entry points than the interface specification declares. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004) integrity path is held to the same rule. Neither has been through the review that would establish the bound, and the interlock currently allocates at initialisation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 update format handled by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) has no explicit capability field, so adding a new security function to a future release means either changing the format for every LRU at once or accepting a weaker verification during the transition. The planned format carries an explicit version and capability field, letting a new function be introduced without relaxing verification of the current one, with the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) recording the capability set each release requires. The format revision is drafted and not yet fielded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 records, for each component another component depends on for a security decision, the basis on which that component is trusted — evaluation, review depth, and the enforcement it performs. The map is complete for mission computing: the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) trustworthiness basis is the hardware root of trust and its reviewed verification path, and the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) basis is its module validation plus the reviewed key release precondition. The Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) is the gap: it is depended on for an authorization decision but its supplier assurance case has not been delivered, so the rule that it must not accept an authorization from a component with a weaker basis cannot yet be evaluated. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 platform trust is rooted in the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) hardware root of trust, and the intended rule is that nothing is trusted by something below it in the boot chain — in particular the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) should refuse to release key material to a caller whose boot measurement is absent. Today the module releases keys on a caller identity check alone, so the hierarchy is asserted by the boot design but not enforced at the key boundary. The measurement precondition is specified for the next module firmware release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Modification of the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) currently requires the same signing authority as a mission application update, so the components carrying the most platform trust are no harder to change than the ones carrying the least. No graded modification authority exists and none has been designed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Mission applications on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) presently obtain some protected services from peers at their own trust level, which means a higher-trust function can depend on a lower-trust provider. The planned rule is that a component obtains protection only from a component at or above its own trust level, and that the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) — the highest-trust element in the payload path — depends on nothing below it. The service placement change is designed and not yet applied. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The set of WS-X90 elements that must be trusted for a payload command to be authorised is intended to be exactly two — the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) and the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) — with any addition to that set requiring an architecture change decision rather than a code review. Today the set is three, because the payload interface controller also holds a residual authorization check inherited from an earlier design. Removing it is planned for the next payload firmware release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every WS-X90 platform service runs with the narrowest privilege set that lets it complete its function, and the rule is enforced rather than reviewed: each service ships with a manifest declaring the privileges it needs, the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) compares that manifest against the approved baseline at service start and refuses to launch a service requesting a privilege the baseline does not grant, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) applies the same check to technician sessions so a maintenance session cannot acquire a privilege beyond the one its task declares. Mission applications on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) run under the same manifest mechanism. Refusals are logged with the requested privilege, which is what makes privilege creep visible in the platform log rather than at the next review. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Payload release on WS-X90 is authorised by a single authority today. Two-authority concurrence at the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) has been raised as a design option and rejected for the current build on schedule grounds; no dual-authority mechanism exists in the interlock or in the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010). This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Timing Receiver (LRU-005) currently passes an external timing solution through with a quality flag, which makes the platform's timing trustworthiness a function of the external source's continued correctness. The planned behaviour makes the receiver self-reliant: on loss of the external reference, or on disagreement between the reference and the internal holdover beyond the declared tolerance, it enters holdover and marks its output degraded rather than passing unvalidated time to the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) and the platform log. The holdover discipline is specified and the disagreement threshold is agreed; the firmware change is not built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 composes with external mission systems across the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) boundary, and no analysis has been performed of the security policy that results from that composition — each side's policy is documented, the composed policy is not. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Channels on WS-X90 are authenticated before they carry anything. Across the platform boundary, the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) wired path and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) mission link both complete mutual authentication using key material held in the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and fail closed if authentication does not complete — there is no unauthenticated fallback and no plaintext bypass for degraded operation. Internally, traffic between the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) and the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) runs on a channel bound to the LRU identity established at boot, so a substituted or spoofed LRU cannot present itself as the payload interface even from inside the airframe. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Protection of stored security material on WS-X90 is continuous across power state changes for the mission computing path: the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) exposes no plaintext at any point in the boot sequence before the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) has established the platform integrity state, and a cold start that fails verification leaves the material sealed. The gap is the payload interface cold start, which uses a separate power domain that comes up before the platform integrity state is established; the material it reads is not sensitive today, but the sequence means the property cannot be claimed platform-wide. Resequencing the payload domain is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Telemetry produced by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) is protected in transit, but its metadata — labels, timestamps and source identifiers — is carried in the clear alongside it, which leaks payload activity patterns to anything that can observe the export path even when the payload content is protected. The planned change protects metadata to the same level as the telemetry content on the path to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), including binding the source identifier so it cannot be rewritten in transit. The change is specified and not built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Neither the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) nor the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) currently checks its own integrity-check function; a fault that disabled the check would present as a stream of passing results. The planned behaviour has each run a self-check of its own checking function at least once per mission phase and report the outcome to the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), so a silent failure of the check becomes an observable absence of a report. The self-check design is agreed and unbuilt. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Security-relevant actions on WS-X90 are attributable to an identified actor and traceable to the component that performed them, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) resolves component identity from the record rather than inferring it from the source address. The Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) has been changed to stamp its records with a resolvable identity and that build is fielded. The collector side is not finished: its identity resolution table has not been populated for payload sources, so LRU-012 records currently resolve to a subsystem rather than to the unit, and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) retains the records at full fidelity meanwhile so the trace can be completed retrospectively once the table lands. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Configurable security options on WS-X90 ship in their restrictive state, and the rule is enforced at intake: a baseline entering the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with a permissive default is rejected, and the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) restores the restrictive state on recovery so a recovered unit is not more permissive than a delivered one. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) reports any runtime deviation from the restrictive default. Coverage is not complete: the intake check runs against mission computing and platform management baselines but not against ground support tooling baselines, so a permissive default in the provisioning toolchain would pass intake unnoticed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 fails into a state that grants no capability rather than into a permissive one. The Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) halts on a failed integrity check without passing control, and that behaviour is verified.
