The Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) is designed to remain closed through a failure rather than defaulting open, but the fail-closed test has not been run on the fielded interlock build, so the behaviour is designed and not demonstrated. On the recovery side, the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) restores from a signed image held in the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and stops rather than proceeding when it cannot verify the source; that path is verified for mission computing and has not been exercised for the payload interface. Availability for WS-X90 is moderate, so recovery is a controlled, attended action rather than an automatic failover. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No analysis has been performed of the cost to an adversary of defeating a WS-X90 protection relative to the value of what it protects, and no protection has been selected or sized on that basis. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 protections have not been assessed for their effect on mission performance, and no performance budget has been allocated to security functions on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) or the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) command path. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 maintenance and provisioning interfaces have not been reviewed for the errors a technician is likely to make under field conditions, and no human factors input has been taken on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) session flow or the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) tooling. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No assessment has been made of whether WS-X90 security controls are acceptable to the technicians and operators who must work with them, and no data exists on where the controls are being worked around in the field. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Provisioning a WS-X90 LRU is currently done from a written work instruction that leaves several steps to technician judgement, so two runs of the same provisioning can produce different recorded outcomes. The planned change makes provisioning a numbered procedure executed from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) whose steps produce the same recorded outcome on repetition, with each run writing a provisioning record to the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) that names the procedure revision it followed. The procedure is drafted and not yet in use. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 ground support procedures apply the same ceremony regardless of what they touch, which makes the high-consequence ones no more rigorous than a read-only diagnostic and encourages technicians to treat all of them lightly. The planned change grades rigour by the trust of the component touched: a procedure that writes to the Secure Boot Controller requires two-person execution from the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), while a read-only diagnostic from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) does not. The grading is drafted against the component trust levels and is not yet in the procedure set. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A WS-X90 modification currently leaves the platform in a state that is verified only at the next boot, so there is a window between applying a change and confirming the platform is still in a known protection state. The planned change has the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) re-establish the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) measurement chain and confirm it before the modified image is allowed to run operationally, closing that window. The sequence change is designed and not yet fielded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 design documentation in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) is sufficient for the teams that wrote it but not for an independent engineer: several enforcement decisions can only be located by reading source. The planned standard is that the documentation set lets an independent engineer determine, without source access, which component enforces each security decision and what that component does when the decision denies — with the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) session controls as the first section rewritten to that standard. The standard is agreed and the rewrite has not started. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 depends on two external services: the off-platform archive that receives exported records from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), and the release signing service that populates the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) with signed release metadata. The signing service operates under a documented control set with named oversight roles on both sides, and its compliance is reviewed at each release. The log archive is the gap: the service agreement exists but no ongoing monitoring method has been defined, so its control compliance is asserted at onboarding and never re-checked. Defining the quarterly monitoring method for the archive is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The two external services WS-X90 uses were onboarded on engineering judgement without a recorded risk assessment or a named approver. Aurora plans to require a risk assessment before any further security service is acquired or outsourced, and a recorded approval from the program security authority before the service is connected to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) export path or the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) intake. Neither the assessment template nor the approval gate exists yet. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Identification of Functions, Ports, Protocols, and Services
n: Providers of all external information systems and services used by WS-X90 are required to declare the functions, ports, protocols and services their service requires. On the wired path this is automated: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) rule set is generated from the declarations and reconciled against the deployed configuration at each release, so an external flow absent from a declaration cannot be permitted. On the tactical link it is not: the provider of the service reached through the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) supplies its waveform service and message set declaration as a document, and reconciliation against the radio's configured service list is a manual pre-deployment step that has been missed once. Automating the radio reconciliation is the open action, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) export destination declaration is folded into the same reconciliation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Establish and Maintain Trust Relationship with Providers
n: Aurora's relationships with the WS-X90 external log archive and release signing providers rest on service agreements that state availability and support terms but not the security properties the program actually relies on. The planned change documents, per provider, the trust conditions the relationship depends on — key custody for the signing service, retention and access constraints for the archive — and reviews them when either side changes. The trust statements are drafted and unsigned. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Processing and Storage Location — U.S. Jurisdiction
n: Neither the external log archive receiving Security Log Collector (LRU-018) exports nor the release signing service populating the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) carries a jurisdictional constraint on where processing and storage occur, and neither provider has been asked to state its facility locations. Nothing is implemented against this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SA-10 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every WS-X90 software and firmware component is delivered with a detached signature and a manifest entry in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020); the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) verifies the signature against the release key before staging and refuses any image that does not verify, so an unsigned or altered image never reaches a target LRU. Verification is repeated at execution: the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) measures each firmware image at every boot and records the measurement, which detects a modification made after staging and before execution — the window that staging-time verification alone leaves open. Both halves are fielded and exercised at each release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) reads a supplier-provisioned hardware identity from each LRU at power-on and compares it against the accepted inventory, raising a fault within one power-on cycle for any unit whose identity is absent, unreadable or unmatched; the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) supplies the platform measurement the comparison is anchored to. The check is live for the mission computing and platform management LRUs, whose suppliers fit the identity part. Navigation, timing and payload interface LRUs do not carry it — those suppliers were on contract before the requirement was placed — so for six units the inventory comparison falls back to a serial number read from a maintenance record, which detects a swap only if someone updates the record. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Change requests against WS-X90 configuration items in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) are today reviewed for engineering impact and schedule; security review happens when the engineer raising the change thinks to ask for it. The planned change makes a recorded security disposition from a named System Security Engineer a required field before a change can be approved for build, with the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) inventory reflecting only changes that carry one. The workflow change is specified and not yet configured in the repository. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SA-11 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Mission and platform software entering the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) has passed a static analysis run performed on the exact source revision that was built — the pipeline rejects a submission whose analysis run cites a different revision hash, which is what stops a clean scan of an older tree being reused. Every high-severity finding is either fixed before release or carries a recorded engineering disposition naming the reviewer and the reason; the disposition list is reviewed at each release rather than accumulating. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) software is the largest body covered, and the analysis configuration itself is a controlled item so a rule set cannot be quietly narrowed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 holds a threat model for each external and payload interface stating the assumed adversary access, the component that mediates it, and the analysis outcome for each identified attack path. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) model is current and was re-run when the external rule generation changed. The payload models are the shortfall: the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) and Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) models are drafted but have not been through review, so their identified attack paths carry no agreed disposition and the interlock's independence claim has not been challenged by anyone outside the design team. Review of both payload models is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The WS-X90 mission software toolchain is pinned by version and configuration in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), a build is reproducible from the recorded tool set, and a toolchain change goes through review as a controlled change with its own impact statement; the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) will only run a build from a pinned toolchain record. Payload interface firmware is the exception: it is still built by the supplier on an unpinned vendor toolchain, so those builds are not reproducible on Aurora's side and a tool change there arrives without notice. Bringing the payload firmware build onto a pinned toolchain is on contract and not yet delivered. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has no recorded criticality analysis; component importance is understood informally and is not stated at design reviews. The planned analysis ranks components by the consequence of their failure or subversion at each design review decision point, and places the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011), Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) in the highest tier with the protection measures each tier attracts named explicitly. The rigour is agreed and the first analysis has not been performed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 release candidates are not scanned against their declared component inventory for known vulnerabilities before release; vulnerability information reaches the program through the flaw remediation process after fielding. The planned change scans each release candidate against the inventory held with the release in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), assesses exploitation potential in the WS-X90 configuration rather than in the abstract, and delivers the output and proposed mitigations to the Product Security Engineer before release, with the results also exported to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) for trend visibility. Nothing is running yet. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Technicians are trained on WS-X90 ground support tooling by Aurora staff using material assembled internally; the suppliers of the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) and the ground support tooling provide no training of their own, so the security functions those products expose and their failure behaviour are taught second-hand. The planned change puts supplier-delivered hands-on training on contract, completion of which is a precondition for issuing a maintenance credential usable from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) or the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017). The training requirement is drafted and not placed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Developer Security and Privacy Architecture and Design
n: The WS-X90 design specification carries a complete allocation table mapping every tailored control to a physical or logical component, and it describes how the mediation points combine — the Mission Computer (LRU-001) service manifest check, the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) boundary decision and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) authorization — into a single protection story rather than three independent ones. The allocation table is complete and reviewed. The composition narrative is not: the section that explains how the payload interface protections combine with the mission computing ones is outstanding, so the architecture currently reads as two well-described halves with an undescribed seam between them, which is where an assessor would expect to find the gap. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Commit and signing authority over WS-X90 mission software and Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) firmware is granted on team membership; the access authorization the role requires is verified once at onboarding and not re-checked when someone moves between roles. The planned change verifies the authorization before signing authority is issued and re-verifies it whenever the role changes, with the authority record held against the developer identity used by the signing service. The verification step is agreed with the supplier and not yet in force. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The component inventory held by the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) carries a vendor support end date for hardware and software items, and any item within 12 months of that date is surfaced on the replacement or alternative-support list before support lapses. Dates are populated for mission computing, communications and platform management items. Navigation and timing are the gap: the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and Timing Receiver (LRU-005) entries carry no support end date because the supplier has not stated one, which means the two items with the shortest expected production life are the two the program cannot schedule against. Obtaining the dates is on contract; the technology refresh plan is blocked behind them. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
Resiliency goals, objectives and techniques are recorded in the SSP; the design review of the remaining approaches is planned for Block 1.1.
n2: Planned: The mission must keep flying through a compromised element; the program designs for cyber resiliency against the goals, objectives, techniques, approaches and principles set below.

n: SC-1 is carried as data rather than as a filing cabinet: the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) stores the WS-X90 system and communications protection policy and its procedures as signed baseline objects with issue date, owner and supersession history, and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) reads that issue date when it assembles a release and refuses to build against a baseline older than 12 months. What is missing is the review itself - the annual reissue is a calendar item held by the security engineering lead, not a workflow with a recorded decision, so the check enforces freshness of the artifact without evidencing that a review took place. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Separation of System and User Functionality
n: User-facing mission function and system management function are separated on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) by the partition table in the approved build: mission applications and the platform management agent hold distinct memory-protected partitions with their own scheduling budgets and no shared writable region, and the management-plane socket is not visible from a mission partition. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) binds its service endpoints to the management interface alone, so the separation holds at both ends rather than depending on the caller behaving. Rejections are counted on LRU-001 so an attempt is visible rather than silent. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Security functions are isolated on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) by a dedicated partition whose image and partition table are measured and locked by the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) during authenticated boot, and by delegating all key use to the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) so key material never enters the mission address space. The isolation is asserted at the memory-protection and boot-measurement level. It is not complete: the last-level cache is shared between the security partition and mission workloads with no way partitioning, so a timing side channel between them is not excluded, and the isolation analysis carries that as an open item pending a processor configuration change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Residual information in shared resources is handled on the release path, not the allocation path: the Mission Computer (LRU-001) fills a shared buffer with the approved pattern as it is released back to the pool, and the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) does the same for storage blocks and refuses to issue a block its free-pool metadata does not mark cleared. Placing the clear at release removes the race where a fast consumer reads a block before an allocation-time clear runs. Byte-level comparison after re-issue is part of the build acceptance test rather than a one-off check. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Denial-of-service effects are limited at two points: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) polices each external interface to the approved traffic profile ahead of its session table so a flood is dropped before it consumes session state, and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) applies per-port storm control so an internal flood cannot starve the payload command segment. What is missing is the resource side of the control: LRU-007 does not yet export session-table and buffer occupancy, so the program can show that flooding is shed but cannot show how close the platform came to exhaustion during the event. Consistent with the moderate availability categorization no redundant ingress path exists. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Restrict Ability to Attack Other Systems
n: Restricting the platform's ability to attack other systems is enforced at the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) rather than trusted to the on-platform sender: egress is policed per external destination and matched against the approved flow list, and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) will only transmit what the gateway hands it, so no on-platform process has an independent path off the platform. The gap is the shape of the policer - it counts per destination, so a compromised process that spreads a low-rate flood across many destinations stays under every individual cap. An aggregate egress budget is on the gateway configuration backlog. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Capacity and bandwidth management for WS-X90 is planned, not built. The design intent is a recorded reserve on each Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) segment and a stated link budget and queue behaviour for the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), both sized against the worst-case mission traffic profile and held in the approved configuration baseline so a configuration change that eats the reserve is visible. Because the system is categorized moderate for availability the approach is provisioning and documented degradation, not redundancy: the analysis will say what is lost when a link is lost rather than claim a failover the platform does not have. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Detection and monitoring of denial-of-service indicators runs between two LRUs: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) samples per-interface utilisation, connection-rate and drop counters and exports them every 60 seconds with a sequence number, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) holds the threshold state and raises one alert per sustained excursion instead of one per sample. The gap is on the resource side of the enhancement - LRU-007 does not export session-table or buffer occupancy, so an attack that exhausts state at a low packet rate would not show in the exported set. Adding those counters is scheduled with the next gateway telemetry change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SC-7 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The number of external connections is held at two by construction rather than by policy: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) is the only LRU with an interface in the external address space, carrying the ground data link and the maintenance service port, and every other external-capable interface in the platform hardware is administratively down in the fielded baseline with its state measured at boot. The interface inventory is checked against the baseline as part of configuration verification, so a third connection cannot appear without an approved change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Each external telecommunication service terminates on its own managed interface of the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) under a named traffic-flow policy, with confidentiality and integrity provided on the wire and inbound routing and control-plane protocol traffic filtered before any forwarding decision; the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) presents its link through that same policy and cannot originate traffic outside it. Two parts of the enhancement are open: the outbound publication that would let a remote network detect unauthorized control-plane traffic coming from WS-X90 is not built, and the exception review described in the companion requirement is still manual. This narrative is synthetic demo content. Exceptions to a traffic-flow policy are held as objects in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) rather than as comments in a rule set, each with the mission justification, the duration of the need, an owner and a last-review date, and the review interval is the 180 days that CNSSI 1253 carries for this enhancement. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) is designed to refuse a gateway build containing a stale exception but that check is not yet enforcing, so today the interval is kept by a scheduled manual review. Until the check is switched on, an expired exception could reach a build. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Deny by Default — Allow by Exception
n: Deny by default is enforced at both boundary layers. Every interface rule set on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and every port and segment rule set on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) ends in a counted deny, in both directions, and the approved flow list is the only thing that opens a path. The counters matter as much as the deny: a dropped packet is attributable to an interface and a direction, which is what makes an unexpected drop investigable rather than invisible. A rule-set review against the baseline is part of configuration verification and looks specifically for permit-any rules. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Split tunnelling is prevented for the one remote-device case WS-X90 has: a Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) connected to the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014). The laptop baseline leaves only the maintenance interface enabled during a session, a posture agent enumerates active interfaces at establishment and every 60 seconds, and LRU-014 drops the session within 5 seconds of a report showing a second interface. The weakness is the trust model: the evidence is the endpoint's own report, so an operator with local control of LRU-019 could suppress it. Independent verification from the gateway side is on the maintenance access backlog. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Route Traffic to Authenticated Proxy Servers
n: Traffic bound for networks outside Aurora Defense Systems' control is routed through the authenticated proxy on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007), which terminates and re-originates the session so no on-platform host holds a connection to an untrusted network; exemptions exist only as named entries carrying a reference to the authorizing official's decision. The gap is a real one rather than a paperwork one: firmware retrieval over the maintenance service port still uses an unproxied path, so the exemption set in practice is wider than the named list. Moving that retrieval behind the proxy is the remediation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Outgoing traffic that would threaten an external system is dropped at the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) against the approved egress threat rules, and the gateway resolves the source address to an originating LRU and partition before sending a denial record to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) inside 60 seconds. The auditing half of the enhancement is incomplete: when the traffic originates from a maintenance session the record names the Maintenance Access Gateway rather than the operator behind it, so attribution stops at a device. Carrying the maintenance session identity forward into the gateway record is the fix. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Exfiltration prevention on WS-X90 is a type check plus a cryptographic gate: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) classifies each outbound object against the approved mission data type list and blocks anything unmatched, and it refuses to transmit an object that has not been wrapped by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) under the mission key in force, with the key identifier recorded in the wrap. The enhancement also calls for exfiltration testing, and that is where the program is short: one test has been run against the ground data link, there is no recurring cadence, and the maintenance service port has not been tested at all. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Incoming traffic is constrained as pairs rather than as a source list: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) accepts only the named ground control source addresses and only when the destination is one of the LRUs paired to that source, and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) re-checks the same pairing on the internal segment. Doing the check twice means the restriction survives a host that reaches the internal fabric by some other route, which is the case that a boundary-only check misses. Both pair lists are verified against the approved baseline during configuration verification. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Host-based boundary protection is fielded on the three WS-X90 components that can run it. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) enforce a ruleset derived from their declared flows, and every other LRU appears on an exemption list with the reason - most are fixed-function hardware with no host stack to filter. The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is the gap: the ruleset is deployed but running in log-only mode pending a field trial, so on the one endpoint that leaves the hangar the filter currently observes rather than blocks. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Isolation of Security Tools, Mechanisms, and Support Components
n: The security tooling - the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) - is separated from the rest of the platform by a management segment on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) with an explicit managed-interface rule set, and LRU-018 binds its services only to that segment so it does not answer on any other. The enhancement asks for physically separate subnetworks, and WS-X90 has a VLAN on shared switch hardware instead: the logical separation holds against a misrouted host but not against a fabric-level compromise of LRU-009. The program has not yet decided between adding a dedicated switch and accepting the difference. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Unauthorized physical connection at boundary-crossing interfaces is addressed with keyed locks and port blanks rather than with detection: both Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) external terminations are locked under recorded key control, unused Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) ports are physically blanked per the inventory, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) service connector is locked. What is missing is evidence of tampering: the LRU-014 connector has no tamper-evident seal, so a connection made and removed between inspections leaves nothing behind. Seals are specified and on order. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Privileged access to WS-X90 is funnelled: the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) is the only path, it authenticates the operator and mints the session identifier, and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) refuses a privileged session arriving on any other interface. Because the gateway is a dedicated managed interface rather than a jump host on the general network, the access-control decision and the audit record are made in the same place, and every administrative action LRU-013 performs carries the operator identity and session identifier forward. The command stream is recorded at LRU-014 in order with results. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Fail-secure behaviour on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) is implemented as a latch rather than as a policy: independent watchdogs cover the policy engine and the forwarding path, either one failing drops the data plane inside 2 seconds, and the closed state is written to non-volatile configuration so a power cycle does not reopen the boundary. Restoring service requires an explicit operator action, which is what stops a reboot from being used as a way past a failed policy engine. The failure-mode analysis enumerates the detected failure paths and shows none of them reaching a permissive mode. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Boundary protection is used inside the platform to isolate the mission-critical payload command function. The Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) carries payload command on a dedicated segment with no inter-segment route to mission or management traffic, and the two LRUs on it - the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) - accept command frames only on that interface. The isolation is structural: a compromised mission host has no route onto the segment, so reaching the interlock is not a matter of defeating a check. Route traces from every other LRU are part of the acceptance test. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Separate Subnets for Connecting to Different Security Domains
n: Planned: Each security domain the platform touches reaches it through its own subnet at the gateway.

WS-X90 has one planned connection that this enhancement governs - the unclassified ground segment link - and it is not built. The interface exists on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) but is administratively down in the fielded baseline with its state measured at boot, and no boundary protection device has been selected for the path. The plan is to select and accredit the device, place it in the path, and only then enable the interface under an approved configuration change; until then the honest position is that the connection does not exist rather than that it is protected. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

No WS-X90 component connects to a public network, and that is enforced in two different ways because the two exposures are different. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) carries no default route at all, so a destination outside the approved external address set is dropped rather than forwarded toward whatever the upstream router would do with it. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), which is where a public connection would most plausibly appear as a convenience, has no enabled interface to a routable network and receives updates only on removable media enrolled in the Configuration Repository. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Critical functions are segmented on the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) and the segmentation is enforced twice for the payload path: the switch has no route from other subnets onto payload command, and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) independently rejects an arming frame whose ingress subnet is wrong, so a switch misconfiguration alone cannot deliver one. Three of the four intended subnets exist. Platform management and log export still share a subnet, which means a compromised management host sits alongside the log path it would want to reach; splitting them is a scheduled configuration change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SC-8 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Confidentiality and integrity in transmission are provided by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), which wraps every outbound frame before it reaches the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) or the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008); both refuse to transmit an unwrapped frame and verify inbound wraps before any parsing happens. There is no unprotected fallback mode: if the crypto interface is unavailable the link stops rather than degrading. Integrity failures are counted and reported so a modified frame is a visible event, not a silent discard. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Pre- and post-transmission handling is where mission data exists in the clear on the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), and the design narrows that window: staging memory is mappable only by the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) interface driver, and the transmit buffer is overwritten with the approved fill pattern on release. The receive side is incomplete - inbound staging buffers are reused without an explicit overwrite, so plaintext from a prior frame can persist until it is overwritten by the next one. The fix is a firmware change scheduled against the next radio drop and is tracked as an open gap. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Network disconnect is enforced on the only long-lived session type WS-X90 has. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) tracks per-session inactivity against the 15-minute value CNSSI 1253 carries for this control and terminates at that point, and it deliberately does not treat transport keepalives as activity, so an idle session cannot be held open by a client that is simply still connected. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) drops the transport state at the same time, so the client cannot resume into the old session and must authenticate again. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SC-12 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SC-13 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 does not implement this control. No collaborative computing device or application is fielded on any of the twenty LRUs, but the two ground support endpoints - the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) - expose audio input hardware that the baseline does not disable, and neither gives a physically present user any indication of use. The program has not decided whether to disable the peripherals in the baseline or to tailor the control out on the grounds that no collaborative application exists, and until that decision is recorded no coverage is asserted. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Transmission of Security and Privacy Attributes
n: Security attributes travel with navigation data across the internal bus: the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) stamps every forwarded message with a source identifier and its own integrity check result, and the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) refuses a message whose attribute set is missing or unrecognised instead of defaulting it, which is the behaviour that makes the attribute load-bearing. The association breaks at the subsystem edge: when navigation state is exported to mission compute the attributes are dropped, so a consumer there cannot tell a checked value from an unchecked one. Extending the attribute across that interface is the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content. On the payload path the attribute that matters is which command authority was in force. The Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) stamps it into every command frame and discards returning telemetry whose attribute does not match, which is what prevents a stale stream being read as a response to the current authority, and the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) copies the attribute into its health frames. The association is lost at storage: LRU-012's stored telemetry record has no attribute field, so an after-the-fact review cannot tell which authority a stored reading belonged to. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Integrity verification of transmitted attributes is designed and not yet built. Today the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) act on attribute blocks that travel unprotected alongside the message body, so a modified attribute is accepted at face value. The plan adds a keyed check computed over the attribute block through the shared cryptographic interface, verified before the attribute is used in any admission or authorization decision, with a failed check treated as an absent attribute rather than as a warning. The change is scheduled against a named firmware drop. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Anti-spoofing of the attribute that says a navigation integrity check passed is not implemented. The exposure is specific: today the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) trusts the claim in the attribute, so an injected message asserting a passed check is admitted to the navigation solution on that assertion alone. The design binds the claim to a per-boot value held only by the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006), tagging each attribute so a claim can only come from the component that could have made the check, and rejecting attributes replayed from earlier boots. It is on the navigation firmware plan and carried as an open risk in the meantime. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Cryptographic binding between attributes and the information they describe is planned. Without it, the attribute and the body are two adjacent fields, and a bus participant able to assemble a message can pair a genuine attribute block with a body of its choosing. The design has the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) sign the concatenation of the attribute block and the body and the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) verify it before use. The open engineering question is rate: the analysis to confirm LRU-003 can sustain the per-message signing rate in the worst-case mission profile is part of the planned work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Certificates come from the approved government PKI under the program certificate policy, and the part that gets checked is the trust store: the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) holds the anchors in protected storage and cannot add one at run time, so the store is what was provisioned and nothing else. The Configuration Repository (LRU-020) holds the authoritative anchor list as a signed object with its change history, which makes adding an anchor an approved configuration event with an owner rather than an edit somebody made. Configuration verification compares the two. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Mobile code on WS-X90 means interpreted and dynamically loaded content inside load modules, not browser content, and it is governed by a dated acceptable and unacceptable technology list with a named owner. For the Mission Computer (LRU-001) the list has been enforced at build time throughout the assessment - a module containing an unacceptable technology fails the build and the failure names it - which is why the airborne baseline can be asserted. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) tooling pipeline came under the same gate on 2026-11-03, when the existing build scan was extended over it and the software configuration control board reading became a record of the decision rather than the decision itself, so both endpoints now refuse an unacceptable technology by build rather than by reviewer attention. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Identify Unacceptable Code and Take Corrective Actions
n: Identifying unacceptable code and acting on it is implemented as a flag plus a refusal plus an action: the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) evaluates each package manifest against the unacceptable technology list and flags the package object, the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) refuses a flagged package, and the refusal opens a control board item with an owner so it cannot simply be retried. The limit is that the check reads manifests, not content, so a package that under-declares what it contains passes. Adding content inspection at repository intake is the identified fix. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Verifying that acquisition, development and use of mobile code meets the category handling rules is planned work. The rules themselves are the ones CNSSI 1253 carries for this enhancement - signed versus unsigned handling, constrained execution, trusted source over an assured channel - and the plan is to make the category a field on the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) acceptance record and to have the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) refuse a package that has none, so the category becomes a gate rather than a label. Today the same judgement is made by a reviewer against development artifacts, with no record that survives into the release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Downloading and executing unacceptable code is prevented most firmly where it matters most: the Mission Computer (LRU-001) has no run-time code loader reachable from any interface and executes only signed modules from the measured baseline, so there is nothing on the airborne side for a downloaded module to run in. The Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) verifies package signatures and blocks failures by default, but an operator override remains available and is only recorded after use, which means an unsigned package can reach the provisioning chain if an operator chooses. Removing that override is the tracked remediation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Automatic execution of embedded code is blocked on the two WS-X90 endpoints that handle documents at all - the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) - across the application scope CNSSI 1253 names for this enhancement. A document with an embedded construct opens with it disabled, the policy is set in the approved baseline and is not locally changeable, and enabling a construct is an explicit operator action that produces a record naming the file, the construct and the operator. On LRU-017 the same action also raises a review item if the file is inside a package under assembly, so a provisioning artifact cannot quietly acquire an enabled construct. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Secure name resolution from the authoritative source is planned. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) already serves the internal WS-X90 name space and the zone content is under configuration control, but responses carry no origin-authentication or integrity artifact, so the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) accepts them on the basis of where they came from. The planned work selects the artifact format and the key holder, enables signing on LRU-013, and switches LRU-007 to discard unsigned responses at the same time. WS-X90 operates one flat internal zone with no child zones, so the chain-of-trust element of the control has no delegation to cover. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Secure Name/Address Resolution Service (Recursive or Caching Resolver)
n: The resolver on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) has recursion disabled and exactly one permitted upstream, the internal authoritative service, and discards responses arriving from anywhere else; the Mission Computer (LRU-001) has that resolver as its only configured address with no fallback entry, so a failed resolution fails rather than escaping to another path. What is not implemented is the verification the control asks for: no origin authentication or integrity check is performed on the response, because the authoritative side does not yet produce artifacts to check. The two gaps close together. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Architecture and Provisioning for Name/Address Resolution Service
n: Architecture and provisioning for name resolution is planned. Today a single instance on the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) holds both the authoritative and resolving roles, which means a resolver-side compromise reaches the zone content. The plan splits them into two instances on separate Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) segments, with the resolver holding no zone and no write path. Fault tolerance is deliberately scoped to the moderate availability categorization: the second instance exists for role separation, and the design record states plainly that losing an instance degrades resolution rather than failing over, so nobody reads redundancy into it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SC-23 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Session identifiers are invalidated as a positive action rather than left to expire. The Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) removes the identifier from its active table on operator logout, inactivity timeout and link loss, and pushes the invalidation to the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), which rejects and counts any later message bearing it. Covering link loss matters as much as logout - it is the path where a client-side capture is most plausible - and the counter means a replay attempt shows up rather than simply failing quietly. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Session identifiers on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) are generated by the gateway and only by the gateway: a client-supplied identifier is rejected rather than adopted, which removes session fixation as a class rather than mitigating it. Each identifier is at least 128 bits drawn from the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) hardware random source rather than from a software generator on the gateway, so identifier entropy has the same provenance as key material. Uniqueness is checked at acceptance across a large sample rather than assumed from the bit length. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Protected session establishment is constrained to the allowed certificate authorities by chain validation in the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) against the roots in the fielded store, with the authoritative list held as a signed object in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and compared during configuration verification. The gap is in how wide the allowed set really is: only roots are listed, so any intermediate under an allowed root is accepted, and the intended set is narrower than that. Pinning the specific intermediate authorities is the identified fix and is tracked as an open gap. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Failing to a known state is enforced by the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002), which drives the Mission Computer (LRU-001) to the defined secure state - interfaces down, keys evicted, nothing partially running - within 5 seconds of a boot integrity failure or a watchdog expiry, and holds it there rather than retrying, so a persistent fault is visible instead of masked. The coverage the control asks for is all failure types on all components, and WS-X90 is short of that: a failure detected inside a running mission partition is handled by that partition's own handler, which may keep other partitions running. Extending LRU-002 coverage to in-partition failure reports is the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content. The state-preservation half of failing to a known state is handled by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016), which writes the failure cause, the last known good configuration identifier and the platform integrity state into the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) before power-down, and by LRU-015 making that record readable through the maintenance procedure without needing a normal boot - which is the case that matters, since the platform that failed may not boot. The blind spot is a failure during a recovery operation: LRU-016 is the writer, so when it is the failing element no record is produced. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SC-28 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Information at rest is protected across all of it, which is the scope CNSSI 1253 directs for this enhancement: the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) encrypts and integrity-protects every stored object with no exempt type, refusing rather than returning a block that fails its check, and the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) holds the keys so removed media is unreadable even with a compatible reader. Recovery images written by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) go through the same path, so the objects most valuable to someone holding removed media are not the exception the inventory forgot. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Key storage is hardware-protected and is the only place keys exist: the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) holds every WS-X90 key in its hardware key store and exposes operations rather than material, so other LRUs work with handles and never receive key bytes. The fielded command set has no plaintext export path at all, including under maintenance authority, which is the case that most often reintroduces one. The key inventory is reconciled against the store slots during configuration verification so a key that exists outside the store would show up as an unmatched inventory entry. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
Planned: Navigation and timing run on dissimilar processors to resist a common-mode attack.
Planned: Mission partitions run under a separation kernel on the mission computer.
Flight software partitions are loaded from write-protected media and verified by the secure boot controller (LRU-002).
n2: Planned: Flight software executes from write-protected media verified at boot.

n: Mission state replicates to the secure storage module; the payload state is not yet replicated.
n2: Planned: Mission data is replicated across the mission computer and the secure storage module.

n: Planned: Replicated mission state is polled and compared before it is acted on.

Operations security for WS-X90 is an intent in the program plan rather than a practice. The exposure it is meant to address is concrete - Configuration Repository (LRU-020) release metadata names components, interfaces and baseline structure, and Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) exports carry the same information in a form that leaves program control easily - but no criteria, reviewer role or decision record exist, so nothing is reviewed today and nothing records that. The planned work defines the artifact types in scope, the criteria and the reviewer role, and schedules a first review against a named release. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SC-39 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Port and I/O device access on the airborne components is closed in firmware rather than at the operating system, and the settings are covered by the boot measurement, so re-enabling a port on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) is a configuration change that shows up rather than a local action that does not. The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) is closed the same way for storage and console, but its debug port is gated by a hardware jumper that sits outside the measured configuration - anyone with physical access and no configuration authority can move it. Replacing the jumper gate with a firmware setting is the tracked remediation. This narrative is synthetic demo content. On the two ground support endpoints the exposure is removable media and wireless, and wireless is handled decisively: the hardware is removed from both the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) and the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) rather than disabled in software. Removable media is handled asymmetrically. LRU-017 accepts only media enrolled in the platform inventory and records refusals, which protects the provisioning chain. LRU-019 accepts any media presented to it, which means the endpoint that travels is the one without the check. Deploying the enrolment check on LRU-019 is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 runs one platform time reference, derived and distributed by the Timing Receiver (LRU-005), and every LRU that timestamps anything disciplines to it - the Mission Computer (LRU-001) for mission and security records, the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) for payload health readings. The tolerance that matters is cross-LRU ordering rather than absolute accuracy, so the acceptance criterion is a 50 ms bound against the reference held across a four-hour run plus a demonstration that records from two LRUs order correctly. The timestamping inventory is checked so no LRU quietly stamps from a free-running local clock. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Timing Receiver (LRU-005) compares its internal clock against the authoritative external source every 60 seconds, logs each comparison with the measured difference, and steps or slews the platform reference when the difference exceeds one second, recording before and after values so a correction is auditable rather than silent. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004) marks solutions computed while LRU-005 reports holdover. The gap is that the mark stays internal to LRU-004: the navigation output message carries no holdover indication, so a downstream consumer cannot tell a holdover solution from a synchronised one. This narrative is synthetic demo content. The value of comparing clocks to an authoritative source shows up in the audit trail, and that is where WS-X90 is partly short. Audit records stored on the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and forwarded to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) carry timestamps from the disciplined platform reference rather than local counters, so records from different LRUs correlate within the 50 ms distribution tolerance. What the record format lacks is a synchronisation flag: nothing in a stored record says whether the reference was disciplined or in holdover when it was written, so a correlation across a holdover window cannot be weighted accordingly. Adding the flag is an audit record format change. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 does not implement this control. Command and control runs over one path - the ground data link terminating on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007), carried by the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) - with no alternate bearer configured on either, so losing the bearer suspends command and control rather than switching it. The system is categorized moderate for availability and no alternate path has been funded or designed; the program owes a recorded decision on whether the mission profile needs one. Until that decision and the build behind it, the honest position is no coverage rather than partial coverage. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 carries an SI policy issued at system level, plus an implementing procedure set, both signed and held as controlled documents in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020); the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) release manifest cites the approved policy version so a fielded image can be traced to the policy edition it was built under. The review cadence is set at least annually against the CNSSI 1253 national security system parameter, and an accountable official is named in the procedure set. What is missing is the event-driven half: the procedures do not yet define the specific events, beyond the annual date, that force a reissue, and the SI procedures for the enhancements added by the expanded control set (SI-4 monitoring enhancements and the SI-7 boot integrity enhancements) are still drafts rather than issued documents. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SI-2 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) runs a scheduled inventory sweep that polls every WS-X90 LRU for its installed software and firmware version and compares each answer against the approved release manifest published by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016). The sweep runs at least quarterly, the cadence CNSSI 1253 sets for national security systems, and needs no technician present: results are written into the platform inventory record and any component behind the manifest on a security-relevant update is flagged as a deviation. The comparison is manifest-driven rather than signature-driven, so adding a new LRU to the manifest brings it into scope automatically. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Time to Remediate Flaws and Benchmarks for Corrective Actions
n: The program intends to time-stamp both ends of every security-relevant flaw: identification, taken from the advisory or defect record, and closure, taken from the acceptance of the corrective build into the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). Elapsed interval per severity band will be published against a program benchmark in the monthly status export produced by the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013). Today neither the identification timestamp nor the benchmark set is defined in the defect workflow, so no interval can be computed; the build is scheduled after the SI-2 procedure reissue. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Security patches for WS-X90 are assembled by the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) pipeline into a single signed bundle whose manifest enumerates every component it touches; the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) verifies that manifest against the pipeline build record and refuses a bundle whose component list is incomplete, so a technician performs one authenticated action per maintenance visit instead of per-LRU manual installation. The gap is coverage: the pipeline currently builds bundles for the mission computing and platform management LRUs only. Navigation, communications and payload interface firmware are still packaged and applied individually, and bringing them into the bundle is the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Removal of Previous Versions of Software and Firmware
n: Superseded images are not left on the platform. After an update is accepted and the platform completes one successful mission-ready cycle on the new version, the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) issues an erase for every upgraded or replaced software and firmware component no longer required for operation — the CNSSI 1253 scope for this enhancement — against the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015). Exactly one prior recovery image per LRU is retained so a controlled rollback remains possible under A=moderate; every other superseded slot is erased and the action is recorded with component id and retired version string. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SI-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The design routes any object quarantined by the platform malicious-code checks from the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) to an offline analysis enclave on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), with the resulting behaviour report attached both to the incident record and to the flaw-remediation item before that item can be closed. Nothing of this is built: the enclave is specified but not stood up, and the quarantine export path from the collector does not yet exist, so today a quarantined object is held and dispositioned by hand. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SI-4 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Detection output no longer lives in per-sensor consoles: the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) registers each platform detection source and presents one merged view, and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) forwards its network detections into that view rather than holding them locally. Sensor liveness is tracked, and a source silent for more than 15 minutes is shown as unavailable. What is missing is completeness of registration — host sensors on the payload and navigation LRUs are not yet registered, so the merged view is authoritative for the network and mission computing paths only, and an operator must still consult those LRUs directly. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Automated Tools and Mechanisms for Real-time Analysis
n: The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) applies its detection rule set to events as they arrive rather than on an operator-driven schedule, with a target of 60 seconds from receipt to rule evaluation and a queue-depth alarm at 5,000 unanalysed events so a backlog is visible rather than silent. The analysis engine and the alarm are in place; automated enrichment — resolving a raw event to the account, LRU and maintenance-session context that makes it actionable — is not, so an analyst still performs that lookup by hand. Consistent with A=moderate, the collector is a single instance and a collector outage suspends near-real-time analysis until it is restored. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Inbound and outbound traffic is watched continuously — the CNSSI 1253 frequency for this enhancement — at all three points where WS-X90 traffic crosses a boundary. The Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) applies the approved flow policy at the external interface, the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) applies it to mission data communications, and the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) applies it between internal segments. The criteria are the flow policy's own tuples, so a flow with an unexpected source, destination, protocol or direction raises a security event whether or not it is correctly encrypted; encryption suppresses content inspection, not flow evaluation. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The program maintains an approved compromise-indicator list — repeated authentication failure on a maintenance port, an unexpected boot measurement reported by the Secure Boot Controller, and a flow policy violation. When the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) matches one, it pushes an alert onto the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) operator panel within 60 seconds and the alert persists across a panel refresh and a controller restart until an operator acknowledges it, with the acknowledging account and time recorded. Alerting is push from the collector, so it does not depend on an operator opening a view. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Approved external sessions are terminated at the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) so their content is available to the platform monitoring path inside the gateway boundary, with session keys created and held in the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and never written to gateway persistent storage. The gap is scope: only the management and telemetry session classes are terminated for inspection today. Mission data sessions carried over the Tactical Data Radio remain opaque to monitoring end to end, and the decision on whether to terminate them or to accept flow-level visibility only is still open with the authorising official. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Outbound traffic is profiled per declared mission phase at both external interfaces — the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) and the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) — on volume, destination set and periodicity, with an anomaly event raised when observed volume exceeds the phase envelope by more than 25 percent over a rolling five-minute window. Profiles exist for the two most-flown mission phases; the remaining phases run against a permissive default envelope, which is the current limitation, and interior-point analysis on the internal segments has not been built. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Three activity classes raise an alert with no operator query: privileged account creation, security configuration change outside an approved maintenance window, and interruption of audit forwarding beyond five minutes. The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) detects them and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) presents them. The mechanism is automated end to end for these three; the trigger set itself is the shortfall, since the activity classes introduced by the expanded control set — indicator-of-compromise matches and integrity re-verification failures on navigation and timing software — are detected but not yet promoted to automated alert. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
Planned: The security log collector baselines traffic and event patterns per flight phase.

The intent is to use the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) receive chain, which already surveys its assigned bands, as the sensing element for rogue-emitter detection inside the WS-X90 physical envelope, reporting each observation with time, band and signal strength to the platform monitoring path. The observation record format and the monitoring ingest route are specified in the design; the radio firmware change that emits observations, and the detection logic that distinguishes an unexpected emitter from an expected one, are not built. No wireless intrusion detection capability is fielded today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 has no inspection point on the path where traffic crosses from the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) onto the wireline segment served by the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009). Radio-originated traffic is flow-evaluated at the radio and again at the switch, but the wireline detection rule set is not applied at the crossing itself, so a flow that satisfies both flow policies is not content-inspected on entry to the internal network. No design change has been approved and no work is scheduled; the exposure is recorded rather than described as partial coverage. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Security Log Collector (LRU-018) correlates three source classes — platform host events, network detections and maintenance-session records — into one ordered timeline. Ordering is only as good as the clocks, so entries are stamped against the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) trusted time source and any contributing source whose offset from it exceeds one second is flagged in the correlation view, which makes a skewed source visible instead of quietly mis-ordering the timeline. Each correlated entry records which time source stamped it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Where the program designates a maintainer as posing elevated risk, the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) is to place that individual's sessions into an enhanced-recording mode capturing full command transcripts from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) — a gateway-side setting, deliberately not a laptop-side one, so it cannot be evaded by using a different endpoint. The gateway already records privileged sessions; what does not exist is the per-individual designation attribute, the authorisation and withdrawal procedure behind it, and the review interval. Until those are written, no enhanced-recording designation can be applied. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Privileged sessions opened through the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) are transcribed at command level and forwarded to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), which holds privileged-session transcripts in a retention class separate from routine platform audit so they are not aged out with ordinary records. What is not yet working is the out-of-window alert: the collector receives the transcript but the approved maintenance-window schedule is not machine-readable to it, so a session opened outside a window is currently detected on review rather than raised at the time. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Both network enforcement points compare what they observe against the approved WS-X90 service baseline at least daily: the Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) for internal segment services, and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) for services reachable at the external interface. A listening service that is not on the baseline is both written to audit and alerted, and the check is service-level rather than host-level, so an unauthorised service offered by an otherwise authorised LRU is caught. Removal of an approved service produces no alert, keeping the signal specific to unauthorised additions. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Host-level sensors run on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013), reporting process start, privileged operation and configuration-file change to the platform monitoring path. Both sensors are signed elements of the approved baseline, so a maintenance session cannot stop or remove them without breaking the baseline measurement. Coverage stops there: the Update & Recovery Controller and the Secure Storage Module carry no host sensor, which leaves the update and storage paths visible only through their own event streams. Extending the sensor to those LRUs is the outstanding work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Indicators of compromise from the program's approved threat sources are to be held in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) as versioned, signed indicator sets with source attribution, then distributed into the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) detection rules with the loaded version visible in the monitoring view. The repository can hold the artifacts today, but no indicator source is under agreement, no set has been ingested, and the repository-to-collector distribution path is unbuilt, so no indicator-driven detection is running. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Monitoring visibility is taken from the network rather than from the hosts. The Internal Ethernet Switch (LRU-009) mirrors traffic at the mission and maintenance segment boundaries and the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) mirrors at the external interface, with mirror destinations restricted to the monitoring path in both configurations, so a host with no local sensor is still observed. The shortfall is at the payload boundary: traffic between the Payload Interface Controller and the mission computing segment is not mirrored, leaving that key internal interface visible only through endpoint reporting. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SI-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The plan is to publish each accepted security alert and advisory as a machine-readable record in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) — identifier, affected-component list, action class — and push it to an advisory view on the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), removing the manual mail distribution step and letting an advisory be linked to the flaw-remediation item it drives. The record schema is drafted; the repository publication step and the collector advisory view are not built, and advisories are distributed by hand today. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Security function verification runs in two independent places. On the mission computing chain, the Mission Computer (LRU-001) self-tests access decision, audit record generation and cryptographic service availability from the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) at power-on, at transition into mission-ready state and on privileged command, taking the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) reported platform state as a precondition; a failed test blocks the mission-ready transition. On the payload side, the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) verifies its own authorization and interlock logic before every arming sequence and reports the result through the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012). In both cases the anomaly action is to hold — restricted state on the mission side, safe state on the payload side — rather than to restart or shut down, which suits an A=moderate system, and the alert goes to the system/security administrator at a minimum, the CNSSI 1253 recipient for this control. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) compiles security function verification results into a periodic report and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) exports it to responsible security personnel — the CNSSI 1253 recipient set of authorising official, CISO/SAISO or equivalent, ISSO and ISSM. The report exists and is going out. What is incomplete is its content: failed verifications are listed but the disposition of each is entered by hand after the fact rather than drawn from the incident record, so a report can go out with a failure whose action is still blank. Wiring the disposition field to the incident record is open. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SI-7 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Integrity checking runs at two cadences on two parts of the platform. At every startup the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) measures the Mission Computer (LRU-001) boot loader, kernel and signed application set and compares each measurement against the approved release manifest, refusing the mission-ready transition on any mismatch and naming the failing measurement slot. Separately, the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) re-verify their loaded navigation and timing software against stored reference digests at startup and at least every 24 hours of continuous operation, reporting a failure to the platform monitoring path within 60 seconds without interrupting navigation output on a passing check. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

An integrity discrepancy is not left to be discovered on review. The Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) emits a discrete integrity-violation event naming the failing measurement slot the moment a comparison fails, and the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) matches that event class to the on-call security engineer notification route, delivering within five minutes with no operator poll. The notification is retained by the collector, so a platform restart after the violation does not erase the fact that it occurred. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

On an integrity violation in the mission software set, the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) automatically places the platform in a restricted state that permits only maintenance and recovery functions — the deliberate choice for an A=moderate system, where holding is preferable to an automatic reimage — and the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) offers the last known-good signed image for a technician-authorised recovery. The automatic response is limited to violations in the mission software set: a violation detected in navigation, timing or payload firmware is alerted but does not currently drive the restricted state, and extending the automatic response to those measurement domains is outstanding. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Three unauthorized-change classes are raised by the Security Log Collector (LRU-018) as incident-class events — unexpected boot measurements, configuration drift from the signed baseline, and the appearance of an unapproved service — and the Platform Management Controller (LRU-013) incident workflow opens a record for each, so integrity detections enter the same response path as reported incidents rather than a separate engineering queue. The handoff is automated in one direction only: an incident closed in the workflow does not clear the originating detection at the collector, so detections must be reconciled by hand, and the response procedure has not been reissued to describe the new detection-originated entry point. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Every potential integrity violation produces an audit record carrying the failing component, the expected and observed measurement identifiers and the action taken.
