The record is written to the write-protected region of the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015), where it cannot be modified or deleted from a maintenance session, and exported to the Security Log Collector (LRU-018), giving an on-platform copy that survives tampering attempts and an off-platform copy that survives loss of the LRU. The two copies are comparable field for field, which is what makes a discrepancy between them meaningful. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Boot verification covers all devices capable of verification of the boot process, the CNSSI 1253 scope for this enhancement, in two forms. In mission computing, the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) verifies the Mission Computer (LRU-001) boot from an immutable root of trust, extending one measurement per stage and publishing the resulting platform state for attestation; the root of trust is not writable through the maintenance path. Outside mission computing, the Navigation Processor (LRU-004), Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) and Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) each verify their own boot image against a stored signature before enabling any external interface, and report boot verification status at every start, so a failed verification leaves the LRU present but silent on the bus. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Boot firmware on all capable devices sits in a hardware write-protected region. The Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) is the only agent that can lift the protection, and only inside an authenticated update sequence staged by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016); protection re-asserts automatically when the sequence ends, so an interrupted update does not leave firmware writable. Any write attempt outside that sequence is blocked at the device and logged, and the write-protect state is reported as part of the platform state so an unprotected device is visible rather than assumed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

All software and firmware from vendors or sources that provide cryptographic mechanisms to enable validation of code authenticity and integrity — the CNSSI 1253 scope here — is signature-verified before installation. The Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) performs the check using verification keys held in and never exported from the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), against release metadata drawn from the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). An unsigned package, or one signed by a key outside the approved set, is refused with a recorded reason; the refusal is at the controller, so it applies equally to a bundle staged from the provisioning pipeline and to a single-component recovery image. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The intent is for mission applications on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) to carry in-process runtime protections that detect control-flow and memory-corruption attempts, terminate the affected process and raise a security event rather than continuing in a corrupted state. The mechanisms are selected in the design record and a security event class is reserved in the monitoring rule set, but the build configuration that enables them is not yet applied to any mission application and no application has been rebuilt or re-qualified under them. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

WS-X90 runs no messaging service of its own, so spam protection is scoped to content screening at the points where message and file content enters or leaves the platform: the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) for network-borne content, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) for content transferred from the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019). The content policy and the rejection-and-log disposition are drafted, but no screening engine is installed at either point and nothing is being screened today; deliberately, the design places screening at the gateways rather than inside mission applications. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

There is no automatic weekly refresh of a content-screening rule set, because there is no screening engine on the Protected Network Gateway (LRU-007) to refresh — see SI-8. The signed rule package build on the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) does not exist either, and no active rule-set version or refresh timestamp is reported to the platform monitoring path. This is recorded as not implemented rather than partial; the at-least-weekly cadence from CNSSI 1253 becomes a requirement on the build once SI-8 is fielded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SI-10 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Behaviour on invalid input is specified per input class — reject, clamp to a documented safe value, or hold current state — for the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006), the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011), and the qualification campaign runs the defined invalid-input set three times to confirm the outcome is identical each time and that no LRU resets, hangs or enters an undocumented mode. Coverage is uneven: the payload interface and interlock have a complete documented action per input class, while several navigation sensor message types are still documented only as "reject" without stating the resulting output state, so predictability there is asserted rather than demonstrated. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Restrict Inputs to Trusted Sources and Approved Formats
n: Two input paths are restricted to trusted sources and approved formats. The Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) accepts navigation messages only from sensor identifiers in the approved sensor configuration and only in approved formats, discarding anything with an unlisted source identifier, an unexpected format version or a non-conforming length before it reaches the Navigation Processor (LRU-004), which therefore never parses an unscreened message. On the payload path, the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) accepts commands only from the authorised mission-compute source on the designated channel and in the approved format, and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) independently rejects any command lacking a matching authorisation token, so a single compromised path cannot deliver a payload command on its own. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Mission software on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) and command handling on the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) treat externally sourced data as untrusted, decoding it through fixed-length structured parsers and passing it across internal interfaces as typed parameters rather than assembling it into command, query or path syntax. The payload command path has been reviewed end to end under that rule. The mission computing side has not: the static analysis injection rule set is configured but its findings on the mission application code base are not yet fully dispositioned, so some legacy log-formatting and configuration-lookup paths remain unreviewed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Errors surfaced off the platform carry a stable error code and a corrective-action class and nothing else — no memory addresses, key identifiers, file paths or account names — with the full diagnostic detail kept on the platform log path where a privileged maintenance role can retrieve it. The Mission Computer (LRU-001) generates the errors and the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) is the surface that carries them to the operator. The screening is enforced in the telemetry formatter, which means new error strings added to mission software are only caught when they pass through it; error text emitted on the maintenance console path is not yet subject to the same screening, and closing that second path is the open work. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SI-12 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Protected configuration, audit and key material in the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) is disposed of by cryptographic erase — destroying the wrapping key held in the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) — followed by an overwrite pass of the affected region, with the disposal recorded by object class and date. The technique is implemented and has been exercised. The retention side is not: retention periods are documented for audit records and key material but not for protected configuration objects, so disposal of that class is triggered by hand at a technician's judgement rather than by an expiry the module can enforce. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
Maintenance laptop sessions boot a non-persistent image discarded at logout.
n2: Planned: Maintenance sessions run in non-persistent environments discarded at logout.

n: Images are rebuilt from the configuration repository; the signing step is automated for two of three image types.
n2: Planned: Non-persistent images are refreshed from the signed configuration repository.

n: Telemetry and status output produced by mission and payload software on the Mission Computer (LRU-001) is validated by the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) against the published output schema and range set before transmission, and a field outside the expected content is suppressed and logged rather than forwarded, with the schema version reported alongside the stream. Validation today is structural and range-based; semantic consistency checks — a reported payload state that cannot follow from the previous state, for instance — are specified but not implemented, so an in-range but implausible value is still transmitted. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SI-16 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Navigation and timing caches are refreshed rather than allowed to age indefinitely. The Timing Receiver (LRU-005) and the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) refresh cached almanac, ephemeris and timing correction data at least every 24 hours of operation, and both delete cached navigation state at the recorded mission-end transition, so a subsequent sortie starts without the previous mission's position solution available to it. This both keeps navigation data current and prevents stale mission-associated position information persisting on the platform between sorties. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Supply chain risk management for WS-X90 currently runs on the corporate procurement policy, which does not address programme-specific concerns such as who may clear a source into the signing chain. The planned procedure set is programme-scoped, names an accountable official, is issued to the engineering and procurement staff who release baselines through the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) and provision hardware at the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017), and carries an annual reissue plus an event trigger on prime supplier change for a criticality-ranked item. Drafting has started against the criticality analysis; nothing has been issued. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

A WS-X90 supply chain risk management plan exists at revision 2 and is held as a controlled item in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) under an access rule limited to the SCRM distribution list, which satisfies the protection requirement. Coverage is the gap: the plan addresses design, manufacture, delivery and integration for the criticality-ranked items including the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and the Navigation Processor (LRU-004), but the sustainment and disposal phases are stubbed with a forward reference and carry no supplier-specific content. Revision 3 closing those two phases is scheduled and is the open remediation item. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Supply chain decisions on WS-X90 are made today by whoever is nearest the problem, which is why the decision rights around the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) signing chain and the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) baseline gate are not written down. The planned standing SCRM team draws named members from programme security, procurement and firmware engineering, and its first task is to fix those two decision rights explicitly: who clears a new supplier into the signing chain, and who approves a first baseline from a newly qualified source. Membership has been proposed and not yet appointed. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SR-3 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The navigation and timing chain is where WS-X90 is most exposed to a single source. The Navigation Processor (LRU-004), the Timing Receiver (LRU-005) and the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) each come from one supplier today, and there is no signed single-source risk acceptance for any of them. The planned action is a second-source qualification study covering all three, with the fallback of a signed and expiry-dated acceptance where a second source is not economically available, both to be recorded against the parts-list entry before the next production lot is released. The study is scoped and unstarted. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Nothing currently prevents a supplier of the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) or the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) from inferring the programme from the order record and the ship-to address. The planned measures are blind-buy placement — order records that name neither WS-X90 nor its end use — and consolidation of deliveries onto a general receiving address, with the programme cross-reference held only in the internal purchasing record. The purchasing function has agreed the approach in principle; no order has yet been placed under it and the general receiving address has not been designated. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Supply chain security clauses are present in the prime contracts for the payload chain — the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010), the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) and the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) — and the primes are contractually obliged to flow them to sub-tier suppliers. Verification is where this is incomplete: the programme has confirmed flow-down for the LRU-010 and LRU-012 chains, but the LRU-011 prime has not returned its sub-tier clause listing, and one returned sub-tier contract carried an amended notification period rather than the clause unaltered. Both are open with the contracting officer. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Provenance is enforced as a staging gate rather than as a record-keeping habit. Every firmware release staged by the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) must resolve, through the Configuration Repository (LRU-020), to a build record carrying source revision, build host identity and the signing key identifier; the key identifier must match a key trusted by the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) chain. A release whose chain is incomplete is refused at staging, so a provenance gap becomes a staging failure rather than a post-installation discovery. Forty-two releases have been staged under this rule with no bypass path. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SR-5 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Sustainment stock for the long-lead items — the Timing Receiver (LRU-005), the Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) and the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) — is planned at quoted lead time plus six months of consumption, held or contractually committed, with a re-review trigger on any supplier end-of-life or last-time-buy notice. Quoted lead times have been collected for all three and the consumption model exists, but no stock has been placed on order and no re-review trigger is wired into the supplier notification handling, so an end-of-life notice today would not prompt a stock decision. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Assessments Prior to Selection, Acceptance, Modification, or Update
n: Acceptance into the WS-X90 baseline is gated on an assessment record covering supplier standing, signature verification result and known-vulnerability check, and the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) refuses to stage a package whose record is absent from the Configuration Repository (LRU-020). Firmware and software packages are fully covered by this gate. What is not covered is hardware and development tooling: a replacement component or a new build tool is accepted on the engineering acceptance sheet with no assessment record, so the LRU-016 gate never sees it. Extending the record requirement to those two categories is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

The three suppliers behind the Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008), the Navigation Processor (LRU-004) and the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) are on an annual assessment cycle, and the LRU-004 and LRU-010 suppliers have current reviews. The LRU-008 supplier review is 14 months old and therefore out of cycle. The event-driven half is weaker still: the review procedure names change of ownership as a trigger but not a reported compromise at the supplier or a sector counterfeit finding on the same part family, so two of the three triggers have no procedural hook. Adding them and clearing the overdue review are the open actions. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Independent testing of supplied elements is planned for the two items where a hidden interface or a substituted firmware image would be hardest to detect downstream: the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) and the Timing Receiver (LRU-005). The planned scope is undocumented interface discovery and a comparison of delivered firmware against the supplier-declared hash, carried out by a third-party laboratory before first lot acceptance. A laboratory has been shortlisted and the test scope drafted; no testing has been commissioned and both items were accepted on supplier declaration alone for the current lot. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Not implemented. WS-X90 supply chain information — the parts list, supplier names, lot quantities and delivery schedules — is handled at the sensitivity of each individual item, and the aggregate is not treated as more sensitive than its parts. The parts list sits in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) under a broader read rule than the signed release baselines. No operations security analysis of the aggregate has been carried out. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Notification agreements are in place for the two suppliers whose compromise would be hardest to detect from the platform side. The Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) agreement obliges notification of a supply chain compromise affecting the delivered part family within 30 days of the supplier becoming aware, and obliges release of the underlying audit result. The Timing Receiver (LRU-005) agreement carries the notification clause but no audit-release obligation and names no programme recipient, so a notification would arrive at the general contracts mailbox. Both gaps are with the contracting officer for the next agreement amendment. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Tamper protection is implemented as two different mechanisms for two different threat pictures. On the mission computing side, the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003), the Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) sit inside enclosures whose opening breaks a serialised seal, and LRU-003 additionally zeroises key material inside its protected boundary on enclosure breach; seal serials are captured at build and re-read at every depot induction. On the payload side, the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011), the Payload Interface Controller (LRU-010) and the Payload Telemetry Unit (LRU-012) carry a latched electronic tamper indication that survives a power cycle and is read at the next maintenance session, because those units are opened in the field where a broken seal alone would be ambiguous. Clearing a latch requires an authorised maintenance action and is itself recorded. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Multiple Stages of System Development Life Cycle
n: Anti-tamper for the Secure Boot Controller (LRU-002) and the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) is specified in the design review record and verified at first article inspection, so it is not a packaging afterthought. The life-cycle gap is at the far end: production lot acceptance does not re-verify the anti-tamper section, so a change in the supplier's enclosure process between lots would not be caught until the next design review. Adding a lot-acceptance re-verification step referencing the same design review section is the open action. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Inspection for tampering happens twice, at receipt and in the field. At receipt, every Navigation Processor (LRU-004), Navigation Sensor Interface (LRU-006) and Tactical Data Radio (LRU-008) is checked against the supplier photograph and seal serial list before stock entry, and a serial mismatch sends the unit to quarantine rather than back into the stream. In the field, every maintenance induction checks and records the seal serials on the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014), the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) and the Payload Safety Interlock (LRU-011) before any session is opened, so a mismatch stops the maintenance action rather than being noticed afterwards. Both checks are recorded against the unit serial and both have been exercised with seeded mismatches. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
The SYS-WSX90 satisfies the tailored intent of SR-11 through a combination of system-level procedures and mapped component implementations. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Counterfeit detection knowledge on WS-X90 is currently carried informally by two long-serving provisioning staff, which is not a training programme. The planned course covers the marking, packaging and date-code checks that separate an authentic part from a counterfeit, and the quarantine route for a suspect part, and is aimed at everyone who provisions hardware at the Provisioning Workstation (LRU-017) or draws the Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) from controlled storage. Course material has been drafted against the anti-counterfeit procedure; no session has been delivered and no training records exist. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

t: Configuration Control for Component Service and Repair
n: Every WS-X90 line-replaceable unit in the service and repair loop holds an open custody record in the Configuration Repository (LRU-020) naming its physical location and configuration state, from the moment it comes off the platform to the moment it is returned to service. Return is gated: the Update & Recovery Controller (LRU-016) must reflash the unit to the approved baseline, and the Maintenance Access Gateway (LRU-014) must record the closing check, before the custody record can be closed. That closes the gap a repaired unit otherwise leaves — a unit that went to a vendor depot cannot re-enter service carrying whatever configuration the depot left on it. This narrative is synthetic demo content.

Disposal for the key-bearing and storage-bearing units is zeroise-then-destroy with a two-person certificate naming serial number and method. The Secure Storage Module (LRU-015) and the Cryptographic Services Module (LRU-003) are fully covered and no unit of either type has left programme custody intact. The Maintenance Laptop (LRU-019) is the gap: two units retired in the last quarter were wiped to the corporate endpoint standard and returned to the corporate asset pool rather than destroyed, because the disposal procedure treats them as standard IT assets rather than as WS-X90 protected units. Correcting the procedure and recovering the two units are the open actions. This narrative is synthetic demo content.
